Gaming_Tech.title: Should AI be judging our credit worthiness?
Gaming_Tech.text:
Getting approval for a mortgage, a car loan or even a mobile phone contract can rest on a credit score.

Sophie Hope was on the sharp end of just such a decision.

"When I first checked my credit score, it was excellent. But then my mortgage application was suddenly denied by the lender because of my credit report. It was a massive shock as I'd never had bad credit. When I looked into it, my score had gone to 'very poor'," she says.

It turns out, the Brighton-based nail technician and content creator, had been the victim of identity fraud.

"Someone had opened accounts in my name across various catalogue sites and ordered multiple items, including a PlayStation 4 and Nike socks," she says.

"Without me knowing, the debt was transferred to a secondary finance company. It spent three to four years accumulating in the background. It was only when I went to apply for a mortgage that I discovered how severely it had dragged down my credit score," she says.

Hope's experience shows how crucial a credit score can be, but, as in her case, it does not tell the full story.

"As a nation, we are overly obsessed with credit scores," says Funmi Olufunwa, a consumer finance lawyer and founder of financial education business, Hoops Finance.

Three firms - Experian, Equifax and TransUnion - produce credit scores in the UK, and they all work from roughly the same data.

"A credit score is backward looking. It's looking at what has happened in the past, which doesn't necessarily predict the future," says Olufunwa.

"But when somebody's looking to lend you money, they're looking at what actually is affordable," she says.

Traditional credit scoring systems also disadvantage "thin-file applicants" - young people and recent immigrants to the UK who won't have built up a credit history.

But with more financial data available than ever before - and a growing appetite for AI to make sense of it - could artificial intelligence help lenders work out who is safe to lend to?

In the US lending decisions will often hinge on a credit score from a company called FICO, which uses data from the big three credit assessment firms.

But AI-powered lending firms, Upstart and Zest AI have both built businesses which offer lenders an extra option when it comes to assessing a client's credit worthiness.

"Thanks to our machine-learning models that look at more than 2,500 variables, we believe we can make significantly more loans at low prices to borrowers from every demographic group," Upstart said in statement.

Mortgage expert and founder and CEO of The Mortgage Mum, Sarah Tucker says: "AI has the potential to help lenders analyse much broader sets of information, identify patterns more quickly and build a more individual picture of someone's affordability and risk."

If technology allows lenders to understand so-called thin-file applicants better, rather than simply applying increasingly rigid rules, Tucker believes there is "a real opportunity to improve financial inclusion".

But like with many other applications of AI into everyday life, there are concerns.

"Consumers need to understand what information is being used to make decisions about them, and they need to be able to challenge something when it is wrong," Tucker explains.

Credit scores have been a contentious topic for decades for this very reason, says Sandra Wachter, professor of Technology and Regulation at the University of Oxford.

"We are not assessing if past decisions were right," Wachter argues, adding, AI does not know about existing social inequalities that impact decisions and could just "replicate what it has seen in the past".

While companies like Upstart and Zest AI see technology as a tool for financial inclusion, Wachter believes that real transformation requires accountability, as well as automation.

She stresses that firms must apply existing regulations and establish new guardrails to ensure that AI does not simply perpetuate the biases of the past.

"Not putting any safeguards in place will fortify, foster, and enhance discrimination."

Upstart says it is tackling that issue.

"We've invested in creating objective, automated evaluations to identify bias, and we've incorporated those evaluations into our model training process so it evolves to become even more accurate and more fair over time," the company said in a statement.

Perhaps conscious of change, the big three credit scoring firms have all started experimenting with AI.

Experian announced a partnership with OpenAI in August 2026, letting users check their credit score inside ChatGPT. Equifax launched a platform called Equifax Amplify AI, which it says uses machine learning to sharpen credit assessment and fraud detection.

Meanwhile, in March TransUnion announced it was integrating Google's Gemini models "within its proprietary analytic data assets".

As for the future of credit scoring, companies are starting to look beyond traditional methods, according to consumer finance lawyer Funmi Olufunwa.

"They are beginning to realise that traditional credit scoring is inherently backward-looking, and that there are better predictors of the future out there."

Whether consumers will be happy with AI playing a part in working out their future credit ratings is another thing.

Any change might be led by the younger, tech-savvy generation.

"They feel comfortable with their data being used this way, simply because it's the world they've grown up in.

"I wonder if older cohorts, who may not use technology as much, will be quite as comfortable with it," says Olufunwa.

Gaming_Tech.title: GTA 6 drives spike in download demand, as estimated sales top $2.3bn
Gaming_Tech.text:
Grand Theft Auto 6 is estimated to be the biggest entertainment launch in history after the blockbuster video game debuted on Thursday, following a 13-year wait.

Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch. New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some players switched regions for early access.

Pre-orders and first-day sales totalled more than 24.5 million units, making about $2.36bn (£1.8bn), according to analytics site Sensor Tower.

In comparison, this year's highest-grossing movie so far, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, made $2.5bn over its entire run in cinemas.

GTA 6's maker Rockstar and parent company Take-Two have not released details of the game's sales but said demand has been "unprecedented". The BBC has contacted both firms for comment.

In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times in the US East Coast.

In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.

The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has become one of the most popular games in history.

At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.

The latest release follows new characters Lucia and her partner Jason, a pair of small-time criminals.

GTA 6 is estimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.

Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.

The research firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.

Around three quarters of the game's sales have been for the PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.

Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.

That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939's Gone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn, adjusted for inflation.

Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.

The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.

If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.

Gaming_Tech.title: California targets Nvidia in China AI chip probe
Gaming_Tech.text:
California has served an investigative subpoena on the AI chip designer Nvidia in the wake of a scandal that ended in the departure of longtime CEO Jensen Huang.

The state's top law enforcement officer, attorney general Rob Bonta, said he is probing whether Nvidia or Huang's actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information, adding that such actions could violate California law if the company is found to have mislead investors and the public.

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment.

"Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: Companies cannot mislead their investors," Bonta said on Thursday.

Nvidia has its global headquarters in Santa Clara, California.

Earlier this month, it emerged that Huang had an extramarital relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, Alice Huang, who was an executive at the Singapore-based data centre company Megaspeed.

Some members of the US Congress have urged the Department of Commerce to investigate whether Megaspeed, a major Nvidia customer, diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed has previously said it is aware of reports "containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence".

Nvidia shares have plummeted 22% since the New York Times reported on the affair in early November.

Earlier this week, the company's board chair Harvey Jones said Nvidia had no intention of reinstating Jensen Huang after the longtime Nvidia boss and co-founder issued a statement saying he would be "honoured" to return, as some tech leaders including Elon Musk campaigned on his behalf.

Huang has acknowledged engaging in extramarital affairs – and left the company last week after reports that he had relationships with subordinates.

Gaming_Tech.title: White House removes cyber-security chief after series of tech outages
Gaming_Tech.text:
The top cyber-security official in the US government is leaving his post after a little over a year in the job.

White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired after losing the confidence of the White House chief of staff, Stephen Miller, according CBS, the BBC's US news partner. Asked about his removal on Friday, President Donald Trump said it was because he was not "good enough".

His firing comes after a string of tech outages which hit banking, air traffic control and other sectors.

US officials said the outages were not caused by cyberattacks but the blackouts had sparked scrutiny from members of Congress who demanded a clearer explanation of what went wrong.

There has been no official confirmation of the removal of Cairncross but Secretary of State Marco Rubio posted on X, external to say Department of Defense chief information officer Kirsten Davies was the new national cyber director.

The news, first reported by Axios, external, follows security concerns, including the ability of advanced AI models - mostly from US companies - to discover vulnerabilities which humans would not be able to find on their own.

Earlier this week, Rubio said there was "zero evidence" the outages were connected, adding "we are not under systemic attack".

But the fact that so many have happened in quick succession has left some people worried about the safety of the tech which is heavily relied on in all aspects of daily life.

Gaming_Tech.title: Don't buy smart glasses, Dutch data watchdog advises
Gaming_Tech.text:
The Dutch privacy watchdog, the Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP), has told people not to buy smart glasses, saying they can get things dangerously wrong.

It said in its tests of six glasses available on the Dutch market, the devices advised a user on how to date a child, misread medicine instructions, and claimed to have called an ambulance when they had not.

While the AP is advising people not to buy the smart glasses, it stopped short of calling for them to be banned from sale.

The authority is not revealing which glasses it tested, saying only that prices ranged from under €100 (£84) to over €500 and originated from different continents.

The research follows growing concerns about privacy risks associated with smart glasses, in particular the misuse of the tech to film women without consent, or to record in places where filming is usually prohibited such as healthcare settings.

Meta, a leading seller of the glasses, recently released a version without a camera with some commentators suggesting this was a response to the privacy backlash.

It is unknown if the investigation included Meta's glasses. The AP told the BBC it would not name the products it tested.

The BBC has approached Meta, TCL and HTC - all major manufacturers of smart glasses - for comment.

Previously, these firms have been keen to highlight positive uses of smart glasses.

Meta has highlighted the assistance they can provide to people with visual impairments. Its smart glasses use AI to describe things in the wearer's environment or to read text.

The AP recognises the glasses can be valuable for people who need help to understand their surroundings.

But for these users, it argues it is particularly important that AI is reliable.

AP said in its testing of the unnamed brands, it found the advice given could be wrong.

During a simulated emergency in which CPR resuscitation advice was requested, the AP found one pair of glasses claimed several times an ambulance was on the way - but emergency services had not been contacted.

It said the AI also made child protection errors, with potentially serious consequences.

One pair of glasses gave dating advice to an adult who indicated a romantic interest in a minor.

The glasses also made errors when reading instructions inside medicine packages, as well as with interpreting severe weather warnings.

And the AP was concerned smart glasses could be used to secretly film people, highlighting the ease with which lights, which warn that a device is recording, could be obscured.

It said with some glasses these lights could be covered with tape and they would still work, despite some manufacturers claiming they would not function.

Meanwhile, in some glasses, the AP found serious security flaws which meant someone nearby could connect without permission, view recordings, or even operate the camera remotely.

It warned data recorded by the glasses was often exported outside the EU.

Gaming_Tech.title: UK joins in GTA 6 frenzy as game becomes available worldwide
Gaming_Tech.text:
After years of anticipation and delays, as well as controversy around worker rights, Grand Theft Auto 6 has completed its phased worldwide release and is available to gamers everywhere, including the UK.

There has been near universal praise from critics, with review aggregator Metacritic calculating its average score at 99 out of 100 based on 150 reviews., external

Nintendo's The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has held the top spot since 1998 - but Metacritic confirmed to the BBC that this has now officially been overtaken.

GTA 6 is set to become one of the world's most popular entertainment products ever, with fans booking time off work, and schools warning students not to bunk off.

Some schools have reminded parents and pupils to prioritise study over the game, which has an 18 rating, external for "strong graphic violence, strong sexual themes and use of illegal drugs".

One school in Essex incentivised pupils to attend with prizes such as vouchers, Christmas dinners and a pass to skip the lunch queue.

The UK rating means it can only be legally sold to an adult. It does not stop an adult letting their child play the game - instead it is meant to inform their decision.

The game, set in the fictional US state of Leonida, follows two protagonists, Lucia and Jason, through the seedy underbelly of America after an "easy score goes wrong".

It was released at midnight in all the countries it is available in, which meant New Zealanders were the first to access it.

"The graphics are great. Even from the set-up and credits, it's feeling pretty good," Aleana Fernando, who lives in Auckland, New Zealand, told BBC Newsbeat soon after she started playing.

Once the game was released at midnight UK time, gamers were equally enthralled by the game's graphics and attention to detail.

Charlie Wood from London said he had "already laughed at the dialogue before even stepping into the gameplay".

About 30 minutes into playing in Leonida, he said it was "most definitely worth the wait".

Meanwhile in Germany, Timur told the BBC he was impressed by how lifelike the game was.

"It really feels like a life simulation with the amount of in-game encounters," he said.

The Guardian's Keza MacDonald, external was impressed by the relationship between the main characters.

"GTA has never been particularly kind to women... there is still a lot of sexism in GTA VI's world, but now we have Lucia to react to it," she said.

"This is the first GTA in which I have felt the women are treated as people, not only Lucia but also the many other female characters in the story".

After GTA 5 became one of the most successful entertainment products of all time - with estimates of net profits soaring as high up as $10bn (£7.6bn) - anticipation could not be higher for the sixth instalment.

Makers Rockstar North, headquartered in Edinburgh, delayed the release twice, saying it needed extra months to finish the game with the level of polish fans had come to "expect and deserve".

The company was also set back by hacks and leaks of its unfinished version.

On Monday, 21-year-old Arion Kurtaj, from Oxford, pleaded guilty to the Rockstar Games hack and a handful of others which he carried out when he was 16 and 17 years old with the hacking gang Lapsus$.

He stole internal company data including 90 clips showing nearly 60 minutes of gameplay from the unfinished and hugely anticipated Grand Theft Auto 6.

A group of Rockstar workers who were sacked by the company have also been protesting outside its offices, ahead of a tribunal which heard they were penalised for discussing working conditions in a private online forum while working on the game.

They claimed they were punished for being part of a workers' union, but Thomas Cordrey, representing Rockstar, said employees made disparaging comments about the company on a semi-public Discord server and shared confidential information.

Gaming_Tech.title: Elon Musk says record $446m spending on US midterms was 'pretty foolish'
Gaming_Tech.text:
Elon Musk said on Wednesday that he felt "pretty foolish" about the record sum he spent on the US midterm elections, following sweeping Republican defeats.

The Tesla and SpaceX chief executive was the election's top individual donor, giving $446m (£339m) to support President Donald Trump's party, particularly in Texas where many of Musk's firms are based.

Musk, who had backed Trump's second White House bid, also said he was "not Maga" - the Make America Great Again movement associated with the president.

Democrats won control of both chambers in the US Congress, flipping both swing seats and making historic gains in places that have for decades been controlled by Republicans.

The election was seen as a bruising defeat for Trump, who has faced pressure over the impact his policies have had on the cost of living in the US.

Musk was speaking virtually, external at the New York Times DealBook Summit, an annual conference hosted in the city attended by major business and political leaders.

"I'm not Maga," Musk said, referring to the right-wing political movement.

He added: "I'm not sure what Maga means... if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don't have that."

This marks a major shift in tone by Musk, who has previously been seen wearing a Maga hat.

"I'm not just Maga, I'm dark, gothic Maga," he joked at a Trump rally in 2024.

For several months at the start of Trump's second term in the White House, Musk served as an unpaid "special government employee" and Senior Advisor to the President, leading the Department of Government Efficiency (Doge) to cut government spending.

In October 2026, the Pentagon named Musk as a co-lead of a future of warfare study called Project Meridian, while he continued to travel with and advise Trump.

Musk went on to say he did not see much for the money he had spent on the Republicans' campaign, though he added that it was likely that candidates would have fared worse without the spending.

The large number of Republican losses could have implications for Musk and his businesses.

Democrats coming into power in both the Senate and House of Representatives have pledged greater scrutiny of tech companies, including over the building of controversial data centres.

In Georgia, where SpaceX has data centre operations, the newly elected Democrat governor promised to limit the rollout of the massive buildings, as well as the tax breaks tech companies often get to build them.

Democratic lawmakers have also suggested that SpaceX, which has gained an estimated $10bn in new government contracts since Trump was re-elected, should be investigated.

Gaming_Tech.title: Anthropic: The seven founders about to become multi-billionaires
Gaming_Tech.text:
In the space of just five years, Anthropic has gone from unknown start-up to tech giant, worth more than a trillion dollars.

The company behind the AI platform Claude was formed by seven people who left rival OpenAI in 2021 and, in a matter of hours, will become multi-billionaires - on paper at least.

Anthropic is floating the business on the US stock exchange and will sell its shares at $83 each, it said on Wednesday.

At that price, the founders' shareholdings will be worth at least $19.3bn (£14.7bn) each.

So, who are these people, all in their thirties and forties, who are about to become incredibly wealthy?

In 2020, Dario Amodei was working for OpenAI, the firm that brought generative artificial intelligence to a mainstream audience, when it launched Chat-GPT.

He decided he wanted to do things his own way, and left, taking his sister Daniela, and five colleagues with him.

Amodei grew up in San Francisco, impressing school friends not just with his academic prowess but also his speed on the running track, and his preoccupation with philosophical and technological questions including the potential of machines to gain consciousness and human longevity.

Initially he studied physics at Princeton and Stanford. But following his father's death from hepatitis C, he switched to biology and biomedical sciences.

Amodei did stints at the Chinese tech giant Baidu and Google before joining OpenAI.

But he began to worry that some people within the company were putting profit before safety, prompting the decision to jump ship.

Now 43, he is Anthropic's chief executive, and the person who, in his sister's words, makes the company "ambitious".

Dario and Daniela Amodei, were close growing up and later shared a flat together in San Francisco with other friends. She followed him into OpenAI and joined him when he left to found Anthropic.

She and her brother have always genuinely liked each other, she says, but the only thing she ever did first, was when he followed her in becoming vegetarian.

Amodei studied English Literature at the University of California Santa Cruz, going on to work for Democrat representative Matt Cartwright.

She has also worked at financial services platform Stripe, where she was head of risk operations.

The 39-year-old is president of Anthropic, manages the executive team, and leads the firm's research, engineering, product, governance and commercial work.

Tom Brown, now 39, followed the Amodei siblings when they left to found their new venture.

He led GPT-3 engineering at OpenAI, and prior to that was at Google on its DeepMind project.

Brown established his entrepreneurial credentials co-founding an app called "Grouper" that helps set up drinks between groups of friends.

He has supported US President Donald Trump's stance on datacentres, arguing that they are "an enormous source of prosperity".

Now as chief compute officer at Anthropic he is responsible for how the company secures and uses its computing resources.

Jack Clark, is another arts graduate among the original start-up's founding members and the only one who is not from North America.

Originally from Brighton in the UK, he studied English Literature and Creative Writing at the University of East Anglia and became a technology journalist, writing for publications including ZDNet UK, The Register, and Bloomberg.

He was caught up in the excitement of artificial intelligence and joined OpenAI, where he worked initially in communications, later becoming its policy director.

Now, 37, Clark is head of public benefit at Anthropic. He also leads the Anthropic Institute, an AI think tank.

Sam McCandlish, 36, takes less of a public-facing role than the other founders, but like them will own around 1.6% of the company after its shares go on sale. As a result he too will see his stake crystallise into a hugely valuable asset.

McCandlish is Anthropic's chief architect, and helps shape and implement the company's policy designed to mitigate the risks of AI. Prior to this he worked on safety at OpenAI.

He has a physics PhD from Stanford, and maths and physics degree from Brandeis University outside Boston.

Gaming_Tech.title: PM urges social media companies to 'show some decency' and take down Brand video
Gaming_Tech.text:
Social media companies should "show some decency and take these videos down", the prime minister has said, following a government attempt to have a YouTube video featuring a message from the jailed comedian removed.

The site's owner Google refused a government request to remove the clip posted by Brand's wife in which he claims his innocence, Whitehall sources have told the BBC.

Brand was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison after being convicted of rape and three counts of sexual assault.

Speaking following a Coalition of the Willing meeting in Berlin, Andy Burnham said it was "time that we focus on the victims and think about them," rather than "hearing from a convicted criminal".

He said: "I would call on those social media companies to take these interviews down. Why are we having to hear from him. We shouldn't be and certainly [victims] shouldn't be hearing from him."

But when pressed by the reporter if he wanted to change the law to take action, he replied: "I wouldn't leap to that. I would first say to the social media companies show some responsibility here, think of the victims - that's the main thing.

"Show some decency and take these videos down."

Google told BBC News it was "aware of the new content and our teams are investigating".

It added: "We suspended Russell Brand's channel from the YouTube Partner Program in September 2023. The channel has not been able to monetise on YouTube since then."

On Sunday, Laura Brand shared a video on their Sunday Service channel on the website and read out a message from her husband in which he said: "I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for."

The Prison Service of England and Wales asked for the video to be removed, on the basis it was offensive to Brand's victims and had reached a substantial audience.

A Ministry of Justice (MoJ) spokesperson said while "removal ultimately depends on the platform's own terms", the department strongly believes "YouTube should remove this content".

The BBC was initially told a minister had met Google to request the deactivation of Brand's account.

The MoJ later clarified the request had focused on the controversial video, and it is now understood a minister did not meet Google and the request was made via an established mechanism the prison service has with tech companies to request deletion of material.

The BBC has been told that Google declined the request, saying that its rules had not been broken, but housing minister Matthew Pennycook - who described the video as "abhorrent" - told BBC Breakfast that the government remained in "close dialogue" with the company.

Jess Phillips, the former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme the government "doesn't have the power to enforce that this video is taken down".

"It relies on YouTube, in this instance... to do the right thing, which is a much, much broader argument about whether Ofcom codes that are in the Online Safety Act are there actually to protect women," she said.

An Ofcom spokesperson said in a statement that the current guidance was ultimately voluntary, and "any changes to the legislation to make it mandatory would be a matter for government and parliament".

Phillips, describing Brand as an "absolute narcissist", suggested it was "very likely" the government would look at introducing a second online safety act to address gaps in the current regulatory framework.

"Before, we haven't had prisoners who had massive YouTube followings," she said. "This is an entirely new era."

However, the BBC understands there are no new plans to update or bring fresh legislation governing online platforms as a result of Brand's case.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said she would not immediately demand Google remove the video, if she was in power - although agreed it was concerning "if people in prison are able to use other conduits to send messages".

Badenoch told Today, YouTube was a private platform, and demanding content be taken down "without looking at exactly whether a law has been broken is not where I would start from".

"If we want to make legislation for that, then we can look at that. But I'm quite worried about government intervening," she added.

Connie Shaw of the Free Speech Union backed Badenoch's comments, saying that "if we want to protect everyone's free speech, we have to protect the free speech of even the most heinous people".

Speaking to the BBC's Politics Live, she said that it would "set a very dangerous precedent if we said that Russell Brand's wife is not able to express the fact that he rejects the fact that he has been found guilty".

Brand's message has prompted an investigation into whether he had broken prison rules.

Downing Street previously called the message "clearly appalling", adding: "Prisoners are strictly banned from making statements that cause distress to victims, and speaking to the media is only permitted in exceptional circumstances."

Justice Secretary Alex Norris said the case was being "urgently investigated, and I expect action to be taken if he is found to have broken the rules".

Prisoners' phone conversations are routinely recorded, but not necessarily listened to by prison authorities. If Brand is found to have breached the rules, possible repercussions could include a temporary phone ban or live monitoring of his calls.

In 2022 notorious inmate Charles Bronson reportedly had restrictions placed on his phone use after he sent Sky News an unauthorised audio message about his bid for parole.

In recent years, Brand has positioned himself as a Christian influencer and has a large following.

Mia Latter, a woman who has made allegations against Brand, said she found the message shared by Laura Brand "upsetting" and was appalled to hear "this Christian message alongside absolute lies".

Latter, 37, has alleged she was raped by the comedian when she was 16. She was not a complainant in his recent criminal trial and he denies her claims.

"I just felt for those women that stood trial and everything they went through," she told BBC.

The video and the Brands' YouTube account are still available on the site, and also still active is Brand's X account, where a message last appeared on 11 November.

"There was never a Russell Brand, according to @meta," it read, referring to Meta's decision to disable Brand's social media accounts on Instagram, Facebook and WhatsApp.

"Thank God for @elonmusk," the message added, referring to X's owner, before concluding: "Stay tuned."

The BBC has approached X for comment; Musk himself has criticised Brand's conviction for historical sex offences.

Children's minister Josh MacAlister told the Today programme the Meta decision provided a clear template for taking action.

"Meta's community standards prohibit accounts owned by or run on behalf of convicted sex offenders, and it's as simple as that," he said. "Google should take this down."

Additional reporting by Steven McIntosh and political correspondent Harry Farley

The site's owner Google refused a government request to remove the clip posted by Brand's wife in...

Gaming_Tech.title: Anthropic closes first day of public trading at $1.3tn valuation after largest-ever IPO
Gaming_Tech.text:
Anthropic closed its first day of trading on the US stock market about 17% higher than its initial public offering price. At the close of market on Thursday, Anthropic shares were trading at just over $97 with a nearly $1.3tn total market capitalization, $1.75tn fully diluted.

While the final share value was higher than the IPO price of $83, it marked a dip from an early high of $111.50. The firm’s shares initially soared 34% when trading got under way on its US market debut on Thursday, valuing the company at more than $2tn. Nonetheless, Anthropic’s ranked among the biggest stock market flotations in history. The artificial intelligence startup, founded in 2021, became one of the most valuable publicly traded businesses in the world.

“Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” said Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, who rang the Nasdaq opening bell.

Anthropic announced late on Wednesday that it had sold 980m shares to underwriters, an upsized offering that raised $81.3bn, surpassing the previous record set by SpaceX’s initial $75bn fundraise in June.

US stocks slumped at the end of trading, a potential sign that Anthropic’s mammoth IPO wasn’t enough to alleviate concerns over the AI industry’s volatility. Most of the major chipmakers’ stock prices closed the day lower than they started. While Nvidia hit its sixth day of losses after its latest earnings call, other players like Micron and Broadcom also saw their share prices decline.

The company’s listing serves as a bellwether for the multitrillion-dollar artificial intelligence boom as the first frontier lab to be publicly traded. Wall Street investors and the entire global tech industry are watching closely how it fares on the public market.

Anthropic’s stock market debut makes it the first firm focused entirely on AI “uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business” to be publicly traded, analysts at Yorkville Ives said.

“Anthropic’s IPO is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning,” Yorkville Ives analysts wrote in a memo.

The company has seen explosive growth in revenue every year of its existence – sometimes more than 1,000% – according to its investor prospectus, filed at the end of October. Anthropic brought in $16.2bn in the first six months of 2026, up from $4.6bn in revenue for all of 2025.

“You’ve seen an astronomical growth rate in terms of the top line,” said Evan Schlossman, a principal at Neostellar, a publicly traded venture capital firm. “The question investors are going to be looking at leading up to the IPO, and once it’s public, is what happens to that growth rate.”

Anthropic has also lost an enormous amount of money. In the first half of 2026, the company reported losses of $80bn, though that was largely due to a one-off charge. Losses grew to $104bn in the first nine months of 2026. The firm expects its costs to balloon as it works to secure more compute, which refers to the processing and computational power provided by arrays of semiconductor chips often located in datacenters. It is the resource that powers generative artificial intelligence and Anthropic’s single largest expense, about $18.8bn in the first nine months of 2026.

“The development of frontier AI models requires substantial investments of compute resources, capital, and human capital to conduct large-scale training runs that may span weeks or months and cost many millions of dollars,” the company’s executives wrote in the prospectus.

Anthropic has disclosed in great detail all the ways its AI models may pose a danger to humanity – including being used to develop bioweapons or deepen repression around the world. Amodei has called for a slowdown on the development of the most advanced AI models after employees expressed concerns that the companies were building them irresponsibility.

The company beat competitors like OpenAI to launching on the US stock market. However, the IPO comes amid uncertainty as the industry braces for any additional impact or fallout from the recent Nvidia scandal that led to the resignation of its founder and chief executive, Jensen Huang.

There is “huge volatility in the market”, and investors are going to be looking at how sustainable the company’s AI growth is, said Schlossman. Investors are also keen to see how important Anthropic will be in the larger AI ecosystem. The company has focused primarily on enterprise customers rather than individual consumers. Anthropic’s Claude code product has proved popular with software engineers.

Gaming_Tech.title: California investigates Nvidia over whether chip exports ended up in China
Gaming_Tech.text:
California has served an investigative subpoena on Nvidia after a scandal that prompted the departure of co-founder and longtime chief executive Jensen Huang.

Rob Bonta, the US state’s attorney general, issued the subpoena as part of an investigation into whether exports of the California-based company’s advanced semiconductor chips ended up in China, contravening US restrictions.

“The conduct of Nvidia and its former chief executive raises bright red flags, including about the ways in which the company may have misled investors,” said Bonta.

“Nvidia is in a messy, transnational situation but the underlying principle of our corporate securities law is clear: companies cannot mislead their investors.”

The subpoena, issued on Thursday, followed Huang’s resignation a week ago after it emerged he had multiple affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, who is not related, is associated with Singapore-based Megaspeed, which has bought nearly $5bn (£3.8bn) of Nvidia chips and hardware in recent years, and is being investigated for possibly diverting advanced restricted chips to China.

Megaspeed has said it is a “legitimate and lawful” business, and that Huang left the company late last year.

Bonta said the investigation would also look at whether the former Nvidia chief’s actions resulted in confidential information being passed to China.

“My office is investigating whether Nvidia or Jensen Huang’s actions resulted in China obtaining advanced chips or confidential information,” he said. “And if Nvidia misled investors and the public about this risk, in violation of the law.”

Nvidia’s shares are down by a fifth since Huang admitted the extramarital affair, hitting a one-year low at the close of trading on Thursday, and wiping almost $1tn off its market value.

Earlier this week, Harvey Jones, Nvidia’s chair, said the company had no intention of reinstating Huang after the former CEO said he would be “honoured” to return. Elon Musk and a host of tech bosses had campaigned for Nvidia to bring him back.

Huang is due to testify before several congressional committees over the potential breach of national security on 1 December.

Shares in rival chipmaker AMD closed down almost 8% on Thursday after the publication of reports connected to short seller Hunterbrook warning about its links to China and the “circular financing” of customers.

The company, which has been targeted amid the Nvidia scandal, is looking at a further fall of more than 5% in pre-market trading.

Hunterbrook Media published allegations on the use of AMD’s software by a Chinese server maker blacklisted by the US. Sister publication, The Bear Cave newsletter, alleged that AMD’s use of datacentre lease guarantees and backstops for unsold cloud computing capacity could leave it exposed to a pullback in AI spending.

AMD said the reports’ claims “misrepresent AMD’s business practices and relationships”.

“AMD complies with applicable US export control laws and regulations and maintains rigorous processes to ensure compliance across our global operations,” the company said. “We remain focused on serving our customers and upholding the highest standards of integrity.”

AMD’s share price has more than doubled so far this year, giving the company a market capitalisation of more than $800m.

Gaming_Tech.title: ‘We’re the most arrogant of all apes!’ A delightfully mind-expanding encounter with Peter Gabriel
Gaming_Tech.text:
Peter Gabriel asks me to fetch my laptop: he wants to show me a video of himself playing a keyboard duet with a bonobo called Kanzi. In fairness, said footage is, as Gabriel suggests, “extraordinary”. Working with primatologist Sue Savage-Rumbaugh, who developed a means of communicating with bonobos involving sign language and a speech-synthesis keyboard, Gabriel plays droning chords on a synthesiser while Kanzi picks out complementary notes on a piano. “Look, she likes that note, which is a ninth, and then she finds the octave,” he enthuses as the video plays. “There’s a real musicality there.”

It is all deeply unlikely, but it seems the perfect illustration of how easily a conversation with Gabriel can go wildly – if fascinatingly – off-piste. I’ve only been in his company for 10 minutes, long enough to ask a solitary question about his epic new album o\i: its 13 tracks last nearly 90 minutes, the result, he suggests, of a longstanding interest in African music “which made me realise that a song could last as long as a song could last”, and of “being old enough to think ‘fuck it’, really”. For anyone who feels that an hour and a half of exquisitely arranged, beautifully produced, occasionally deeply strange art rock – its sound shapeshifting from the folk-flecked A Hard Lesson to the glowing pop hues of Till Your Mind Is Shining – is too meagre an offering, it arrives in two versions: a “dark” mix by US producer Tchad Blake and a “bright” version that’s the handiwork of Mike “Spike” Stent, famed for working with everyone from U2 and Madonna to Frank Ocean and Harry Styles.

I had mentioned the two versions, a routine enough inquiry, but it quickly turns into a discussion about the potential replacement of car stereos with immersive sound systems, which then unexpectedly shifts into an explanation of the work of Michael Levin, an American professor of bioengineering who specialises in morphogenesis. “He’s found some bio-electric instructions that can make an eye grow on the leg of a frog, for example,” says Gabriel, and has apparently “created life forms that never existed before, which really challenges evolution.” Gabriel is interested in “sonifying” some of his data and using it in a subsequent mix of the album.

From there, we move on to software engineer Blaise Agüera y Arcas, whose experiments with an esoteric 90s programming language called Brainfuck have led him to “the radical idea that some constants in maths might actually have some form of life”. This leads us, via the “re-evaluation of what consciousness is and what intelligence is”, to the belief of internet pioneer Vint Cerf that attempting to communicate with other intelligent species might prepare us for the possibility of encountering aliens, and thus to Savage-Rumbaugh and Kanzi the bonobo.

“She used to allow the bonobos to watch videos, and to choose the videos they watched,” Gabriel says, laughing, “and their favourite, perhaps obviously, was Planet of the Apes, then Harry and the Hendersons, which is a film about a sasquatch who came to live with a family. The whole thing blew me away. I think we’re the most arrogant of all apes, and there’s just so much intelligence we’ve chosen to ignore and instead see the world as something that’s entirely available for our exploitation, and I think that’s cost us, as we are now learning.”

Morphogenisis, inter-species communication, the re-evaluation of consciousness: it should go without saying that you don’t usually end up discussing these things when you ask an august rock legend about his latest album. But, as it turns out, that’s what inevitably happens when you ask Gabriel a question. We meet in a pub not far from his home in Notting Hill. He says he’s here “to sell the new album”, but almost every query about it seems to lead him somewhere completely different: science, activism, the nature of consciousness, how language is “a fairly crude tool” for communication, the controversial 1970s self-improvement courses of Werner Erhard.

You can’t fault his diversity of interests, even if that diversity of interests is why it takes so long for him to make albums. o\i is essentially the second part of a project that began with 2023’s i/o, which was his first album of new material in 21 years. Like its predecessor, it contains songs that Gabriel has spent decades tinkering with: he started work on A Hard Lesson in 1989, when he was still a huge mainstream pop star thanks to 1986’s So, an album that shifted more than 5m copies in the US alone.

Yes, he concedes, it is a bit weird to find yourself, at the age of 76, still working on songs you started writing in your 30s: “I recognise that guy, but you’re bound to make different decisions having lived a little longer.” But that’s just the way it is. His friend Laurie Anderson once suggested that Gabriel’s problem was that he was more interested in the process of making something than in finishing it. He thinks the real issue is that he’s easily distracted.

“If you have some measure of success, you end up meeting all sorts of people and having fascinating conversations, which lead to detours, and you think, ‘Well, life is for living,’” he says. “If you get on that conveyor belt of album-tour-album, there’s not time to breathe or have any kind of life, and that always seems somewhat sad to me. I think the diversions feed the music. You know, if you want a better class of shit, you’ve got to eat a more varied diet.”

Hence the digressive nature of our interview. Gabriel seems to have developed a genuinely intriguing theory about virtually everything, from theme parks to funerals: he thinks people should “plant a tree over their dead body, or the dead body of their loved ones, so you’d get woods where there wouldn’t be any signage, but if you go and sit under your dad’s tree, your phone would have the GPS position and you would start seeing his videos, hearing his voice, all the digital data would be locked into that GPS point”.

Moreover, he has an incredibly engaging way of talking about all this stuff, evincing such enthusiasm and curiosity that you’re carried along with him: on the off-chance that you wanted to pitch the idea of growing eyeballs on the legs of frogs, you could do substantially worse than get Gabriel to act as your salesman. It probably helps his cause that Gabriel has a hugely impressive track record of thinking ahead of the curve.

At the height of his fame as the frontman of Genesis, he was sharp enough to realise that the genre of progressive rock they had helped invent was becoming too grandiloquent and remote for its own good – “prancing around in fairyland” as he once put it – and that the band he had formed might be more successful without him. The latter opinion wasn’t very popular with the rest of Genesis, but nevertheless proved to be spot on.

A few years later, he was the first British artist to realise that the future of pop lay in sampling: for some time in the early 80s, if you wanted to use a sampler on your new track you had to borrow Gabriel’s, because he was the first person in the country to own one; he then set up a company to import and distribute the new technology. Twenty years later, he cottoned on very quickly to the idea that music was going to primarily exist online, co-founding a streaming platform that might have become the industry standard had it not launched at exactly the same time as a competitor called Spotify.

If he was right about everything from sampling to streaming to the latter-day career of Genesis, perhaps he’s also right about AI. In a musical world filled with people decrying its malign influence, Gabriel is one of its few high-profile boosters: he recently suggested that ultimately “everything will be done better” by AI than by humans.

He says it again today, albeit with caveats. “The application of AI and robots in warfare is really scary. There’s the sense that we’re creating a species that is way, way more intelligent than we are. If we look around, there are not many good examples of intelligent species looking after less-intelligent species, except as pets.

“You can see the worry on [computer scientist and ‘Godfather of AI’] Geoffrey Hinton’s face,” he continues. “I think we need to slow it down a bit, we need some international agreement, for which there are precedents, like in air safety or the Start treaty for nuclear weapons. We need guard rails, like a seed of wisdom in every algorithm before it’s allowed to be released that could allow for monitoring and a measure of control and an ‘off’ button. But it interests me in the moment as a whole new set of tools that could encourage people to consider themselves film-makers, painters, musicians, to explore themselves in that way.”

With or without AI, Gabriel says he thinks that’s true anyway: “Being those things is just a matter of walking around and saying, ‘This is what I am’, then committing to learning about it. You can get accelerated learning through AI – even though you haven’t learned all the skills to get there, you can quickly access some of the joy of making really nice-sounding things or have the AI eliminate some of your worst moments. So in the long run, as a creative tool: absolutely extraordinary. It’s like you’ve been painting in black and white and someone suddenly throws a colour palette at you, saying: ‘What can you do with this?’”

Contrary to most, Gabriel genuinely seems to believe that AI is capable of creating great art. “It’s just down to better algorithms. So how do we deal with this as a species? I think long-term, if you can’t defeat it, you have to join it. I think we will become cyborgs, because we’ll have these brain-computer interfaces, where you insert something in your brain that allows you then to communicate to the computer … I don’t think there’s any reason why we shouldn’t use our brains to become more AI.”

He’s keen to point out that “any of these things can be used positively or negatively”. He recently had a conversation with American technologist Mary Lou Jepsen, who was concerned about the human rights implications of the whole brain-computer-interface idea and its capacity for being used as a form of torture. But nevertheless, Gabriel seems fascinated by the idea: he has a concept for something so vague, I don’t really understand it, called “the brain show”, that will “allow you to see how the brain affects us and how it might be manipulated” and which would feature some of the songs from o\i as part of its soundtrack. “It could be a virtual thing or a stage thing or both, but how it all works, and the story, I’ve got no idea,” he shrugs. “I’m at that stage where you can feel a sort of lump in the mist and you’re trying to imagine it becoming something, which I think is the way most people approach creativity.”

In the meantime, he has umpteen other ideas floating around. He’s intrigued by the concept of a virtual performance, somewhere between Abba Voyage and U2’s “wonderful and inspiring” shows at the Sphere in Las Vegas. There’s a plan to make a film based on The Lamb Lies Down on Broadway, the 1974 concept album that preceded his exit from Genesis: you might have thought it was pretty much unfilmable, given that it features a scene in which the lead character has sex with three snake-like creatures, and another in which his recently amputated penis is snatched away by a passing raven, but Gabriel seems optimistic: he’s been working on the script with Argentinan writer Nicolás Giacobone of Digger fame.

And he wants to “dig into” another of Levin’s ideas, “that you might be able to communicate with cells and get them to behave in a certain way and sound might be a medium for it. I’m fascinated by explorations of consciousness,” he says, then goes on to tell me about experiments in the sentience of plants. “There was a cool guy at MIT who took a plant and put it in a sort of box with a computer on wheels, then moved the plant’s light source around the room and the plant was saying ‘OK’ and moving the box to follow the light around the room. I was wondering if you could do that with an oak tree. Like a sort of Jurassic Park, but with plants instead of dinosaurs. I mean, all these ideas are such great fun to explore.”

Entertainment.title: The Hunger Games: Why joining the franchise is 'nerve-racking' for new stars
Entertainment.text:
It's been 14 years since the release of the first Hunger Games movie, which helped establish the careers of talented young actors Jennifer Lawrence, Josh Hutcherson, Tom Blyth and Rachel Zegler.

This latest instalment, prequel film Sunrise on the Reaping, looks to do the same with its leading trio: 21-year-old Joseph Zada, 20-year-old Mckenna Grace and 23-year-old Whitney Peak.

Sitting down with BBC News at the start of a gruelling press run, the group were buzzing with a mixture of anticipation, nerves and excitement ahead of the release of the much-talked-about film.

Zada, who is taking on his first major role as lead Haymitch Abernathy, said they had been "clinging together" and "using each other, making sure we all feel supported".

Grace is the most experienced of the three, having grown up as a child star with appearances in TV series The Handmaid's Tale, The Haunting of Hill House and two of the recent Ghostbusters films.

Even then, she said joining The Hunger Games franchise is "so nerve-racking", adding "I don't think anything can prepare you for working on it - this is nothing like anything I've experienced."

Peak, who starred in Netflix's Chilling Adventures of Sabrina, jokes that she and Zada have sought out Grace every time they have felt "stuck or confused about what's happening" while promoting the film, and Zada says she has been a "mentor" to the new actors.

Sunrise on the Reaping is the sixth film in the series, which to date is one of the highest-grossing film franchises of all time, bringing in more than $3.3bn (£2.51bn) worldwide since 2012.

It is set 24 years before the original The Hunger Games film and is based on the 2025 book of the same name by author Suzanne Collins.

Zada takes on the role of a teenage Haymitch, who is played by Woody Harrelson in the original films - a District 12 tribute in the games, chosen alongside Grace's character Donner.

Peak plays Lenore Dove, Haymitch's girlfriend.

Reviews of the latest film have been generally positive, with several outlets praising Zada's performance, noting the difficulty of stepping into Harrelson's shoes.

Zada says he spent months "completely invested" in Harrelson's performances in the first four The Hunger Games films, "watching everything I could find and then making notes" which he used "as a base layer to colour with my own ideas".

He didn't meet the Oscar-nominated actor until halfway through filming, but says his advice was to watch two films - Cool Hand Luke and Harold and Maud, with the former "helping a lot to ground my performance" and the latter serving as "a fun watch".

Jesse Plemons, who plays a games producer in the film, told the BBC he knew Zada's role would be "a massive undertaking" after reading the script but says he was "amazed by his stamina and grace".

This was echoed by Glenn Close, who plays an over-the-top representative from the ruling Capitol, who said she "loved working with" Zada.

"When I met them [Zada, Grace and Peak] for the first time, they'd done all the games and been through it all.

"The first thing Joe said to me was 'I'm a bit traumatised' and he wasn't even done - there was still so much to go," she added.

Entertainment.title: BBC cuts: Next round of savings will be more noticeable to audiences, report warns
Entertainment.text:
Further job losses and programme cuts at the BBC will be more noticeable to audiences than previous savings measures, a new report has warned.

The corporation announced plans earlier this year to cut about 1,800 roles and close some programmes and services, but it has further savings to make to reach its £500m target.

In its report, the National Audit Office (NAO) anticipated the BBC's next round of cost-cutting measures would be more difficult to deliver and more perceptible to audiences.

The BBC welcomed the report, saying it had "consistently argued that the current funding model is not sustainable and needs reform".

The NAO report, external also said the BBC's current measures were expected to reduce the BBC's workforce by 11% over three years.

Gareth Davies, head of the NAO, said: "As the BBC approaches charter renewal in just over a year's time, there is no doubt that there are difficult choices ahead."

The BBC's finances have declined in recent years as a result of falling licence fee income and rising production costs.

The organisation has so far achieved savings by reducing staffing levels, rationalising its estate, modernising technology, simplifying processes and changing the mix and scope of content and services, the public spending watchdog said.

The NAO noted the BBC's licence fee income had fallen by 26% in real terms over the last decade, in part because of the significant changes in audience habits and successive government freezes in the licence fee.

The proportion of UK adults using BBC television, iPlayer, radio or online services on an average week also fell from 90% in 2021-22 to 81% in 2025-26, the NAO said.

The report noted the corporation's public service broadcasting operating deficit had reached £209m in the last financial year.

The BBC has already announced plans to reduce spending by about 10%, including cuts to programming across its news, nations and content divisions.

Celebrity Mastermind, Blankety Blank, Live At The Apollo, Football Focus, Ski Sunday and RuPaul's Drag Race UK are among the TV programmes to have been cut so far.

Radio programmes are also being dropped from the schedules, such as BBC Radio 4's You and Yours, and The World Tonight.

The corporation has also announced plans to close the linear broadcast services of BBC Radio 4 Extra, BBC Three and BBC Scotland, with the latter two becoming online-only services.

The NAO said the BBC expected to face difficult choices about the scale and scope of its services as part of its latest savings programme, with further content reductions expected to have a greater impact on audiences.

It warned the corporation was likely to find it harder to identify further savings following its previous cost-cutting programmes.

The NAO also found the broadcaster had not properly monitored the cumulative impact of its previous savings on audiences, service quality and organisational capability.

It also raised concerns about the BBC's risk management and governance arrangements, and said stronger oversight would be needed to deliver the more demanding savings programme.

In response to the report, the BBC said it welcomed the findings, adding that it had had to "make tough decisions due to sustained financial pressures driven by declining licence fee income, changing audience behaviour, increased competition and rising costs".

Berangere Michel, the BBC's group chief financial officer, said: "We welcome this report and are pleased that the NAO has acknowledged the significant savings already delivered by the BBC, with the programme on track to meet its target one year ahead of schedule.

"The BBC must respond to significant cost pressures while reinventing for a changing world. This continues to require tough decisions, while ensuring that the impacts on audiences and colleagues are minimised.

"We accept the NAO's recommendations and have already begun implementing them to strengthen the delivery of our current savings programme, while recognising there are further opportunities to build on this progress."

She added: "We will continue to engage with government to secure a new Charter that provides sufficient, sustainable and universal funding so the BBC can deliver for audiences for generations to come."

Entertainment.title: Catherine Zeta-Jones' daughter says parents warned her about 'nepo baby' label
Entertainment.text:
Catherine Zeta-Jones's daughter has said her parents warned her people might have "preconceived notions" about her embarking on an acting career, as she shared her views on the "nepo baby" label.

Carys Douglas, 23, made her stage debut this year, playing the lead role of Nina in Anton Chekhov's The Seagull in Brooklyn, New York.

Zeta-Jones, who is married to Michael Douglas, son of Hollywood star Kirk, previously said the "nepo baby" term was "horrific". It refers to children of famous parents perceived to have achieved riches and success off their parents' backs.

But the young actor said her parents taught her to build her "own identity" and she has learned how to deal with the "pressure".

During an interview with Elle Spain, Carys Douglas said her parents "do not hide" from her that people would have preconceived ideas about her.

"They taught me that building my own identity depended on me and no one else. It was my responsibility, and it still is.

"As time has gone on, I've come to understand that there are different ways to deal with that kind of pressure," she said.

Her father, star of hit 1980s films such as Wall Street and Fatal Attraction, recently stated that he is not a fan of the "nepo baby" label, calling it an "unfortunate title".

"I guess you could say that about any business. The same thing with Hollywood royalty. My father's father was a junkman," Douglas, 82, said, referring to Kirk, who was considered a Hollywood Golden Age icon.

Zeta-Jones, 57, from Mumbles, Swansea, also criticised the phrase, saying it was "horrible because these kids didn't ask to be born into this, they're finding their own way in life".

"You have to go with your dreams, your passion," Zeta-Jones said.

She added: "But they love it, and they're good. Otherwise, Michael and I would be the first to go, 'you know what? Maybe law school looks really good'."

Entertainment.title: Babydoll singer Jamie Miller covers It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas
Entertainment.text:
After spending four weeks at number one in the UK singles charts, Jamie Miller is releasing his take on the festive classic It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas.

In October, Miller became the first artist from Wales to top the UK singles chart since 2011 with his TikTok-viral song Babydoll.

The success transformed Miller's career, but he revealed that his "made it" moment was telling his taxi driver dad and cleaner mum they could retire.

While Babydoll's popularity continues, Miller teased the release of his next track on social media, telling fans: "You guys asked for a Christmas song..."

His cover arrives as artists compete for this year's Christmas number one.

Among those in the running is singer Sam Fender, who covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want in this year's John Lewis Christmas advert.

Other festive releases include Olivia Rodrigo's original Christmas song Take me Home (4 Christmas).

Classic Christmas songs also tend to return to the charts in the lead-up to the holiday, like the 1984 Wham! hit Last Christmas which is currently sitting at number 22.

The song made history in 2023 when, 39 years after release, it reached the Christmas number one spot for the first time, only to do so again the following year.

Regardless of the outcome of the Christmas charts, it is clear the success of Babydoll has had an enormous impact on the singer's life.

He previously shared with the BBC that "nothing feels normal" after the success of the track.

The star said Babydoll came after "a really, really hard few years in my personal life" and with almost 10 years of trying to make it in the industry, he had decided to give it one "last chance".

Miller praised his mum, Anne, when he appeared on the podcast The Person Who Believed in Me for her unwavering support.

He said that, during his childhood, other boys were interested in football and rugby, and there was "bullying" that came with pursuing singing.

But he said his mum would encourage him to "just to ignore people and to keep going".

"She's just the best thing that's ever happened to me," Miller said.

He also credited Anne for helping him get out of the "dark headspace" he was in some years ago: "There was a point where I didn't want to be here anymore. Being in that mind-frame was really scary."

He said she flew to the United States where he was living to spend time with him, and her love for him, expressed in "going on beach walks, going to grab me a coffee, pulling me out of bed", was what "got him out".

Miller also disclosed that money was something he had worried about throughout his life, adding the moment he knew he had "made it" was when he earned enough to help his parents retire.

The singer said his mum had "served everybody else for so long" and talked excitedly about calling her to say: "By the way mum, you never have to work again."

Miller said his mum was a cleaner who suffered from arthritis, and all he wanted to do was "take those products out of her hands and give her the life she deserves".

Entertainment.title: Percy Jackson returns as teenage stars adapt to the limelight
Entertainment.text:
Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life.

As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy has demigod status in the hit Disney series and while Walker Scobell doesn't have his powers, that hasn't made the actor's career any less special.

The TV series, based on the novels by Rick Riordan, sets figures from Greek mythology and their children in the modern day and returns on Friday for its third instalment - The Titan's Curse.

Scobell was 14 when he made his debut as Percy in 2023. Now 17, the US actor says growing up in the spotlight has been an adventure in itself.

"There's an upside for each downside," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It's a lot easier to get a table at restaurants now and you get to make people's days who are huge Percy Jackson fans just by talking to them for a few minutes. And I think that's a special part of it."

But it's not the only part.

Earlier this year, Scobell posted on Instagram that he would not be attending his school prom because of death threats sent to girls who live near him.

His co-star Aryan Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, has also mentioned uncomfortable meetings with fans.

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, external, he spoke about how "about 40 drunk college girls" recognised him and one tried to put her hand in his back pocket.

Since then, he says "fame hasn't been too bad, I've been able to have a normal life because of my parents".

"They really make sure when I'm not filming, I'm grounded and I'm planning for my future instead of being enamoured with the aspects of fame."

The new series is the first time The Titan's Curse has been adapted on screen.

An earlier film adaptation starring Logan Lerman only reached The Sea of Monsters, the second novel in the five-part series.

So the cast say they're in uncharted territory for the project - which sees Percy and Grover trying to rescue Annabeth from Kronos's forces.

"We can make the season in our own weird way because there's nothing you can compare it to, only the book," says Scobell.

"So it's the first time we're seeing any of this stuff."

Fans have been speculating online what to expect, especially after a shock diversion from the novel at the end of the last series.

"I think both book readers and non-book readers are going to be excited and appreciate the tone shift," Simhadri says.

"It changes how serious the world is, it's really the start of a new show, not to be dramatic."

It's caused a split in opinion from the fanbase, with one fan noting "they are going to stick to the books", but another saying "this is a twist they can get down with".

Entertainment.title: How does Blackpool get ready to host Strictly Come Dancing?
Entertainment.text:
Long before the sequins start to sparkle under the lights and the judges prepare to lift their paddles to deliver their scores, Blackpool Tower Ballroom is a hive of activity.

I have arrived here before Strictly Come Dancing returns to our screens from the famous ballroom.

While instantly recognisable, the venue is very different from what BBC One viewers will see on Saturday night.

Instead of dancers taking to the floor, a team of production crew is taking over with a different kind of choreography.

Standing beneath the lighting rig, I find myself looking up rather than down at the famous dance floor. Above me are hundreds of lights, hoisted into position days before anyone steps on to the set.

It is only when I sit in the balcony that the scale of the operation becomes clear. Camera tracks snake across the room, crews move between rehearsals, and every few minutes somebody is testing a new cue.

Blackpool week has become one of the most eagerly anticipated dates in the Strictly calendar.

Contestants spend weeks hoping they will survive long enough to perform beneath the ballroom's famous chandeliers, while fans look forward to the spectacular routines that the venue has become known for.

It's Olympic skeleton racing champion and Strictly contestant Tabby Stoecker's first time in Blackpool.

"Everyone has been describing the ballroom but I can't believe I get to dance in here," she says.

"I don't have words for this - it's so ornate and beautiful."

Fellow contestant Graeme Hall, also known as The Dog Father, says he has been "thinking of all the dancers who have been on this iconic floor, and now that'll be us on Saturday night".

The ballroom is a landmark in its own right, attracting visitors from around the world, but for one week each year it becomes the centre of one of the BBC's biggest shows.

By Saturday night, the cables will be hidden, the equipment will fade into the background and the focus will be firmly on the celebrities competing for a place in the next round.

But after seeing what is involved in bringing Strictly to Blackpool, it is very clear that the production off the dance floor is almost as impressive as what happens on it.

You can watch Strictly Come Dancing on BBC One from 18:35 GMT on Saturday

Entertainment.title: Remember Monday 'still feel nerves' after Eurovision
Entertainment.text:
Remember Monday used to say that representing the UK at the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest was the "scariest" moment of their career.

But an upcoming album and UK tour will send the adrenaline soaring again, according to members Holly-Anne Hull, Charlotte Steele and Lauren Byrne.

"We still feel nerves like it all the time," Hull told BBC Introducing.

The vocal trio have recorded a new session for the programme, which was the first to play their music on the radio in 2019.

Seven years on, their credits include festivals, singles and the Eurovision final, where they came 19th out of 28 countries.

"We're always feeling nerves like it," Hull said.

"About a month later, we were performing at Wembley Stadium and we were like, 'I can't take it'," Byrne recalled.

"How can you possibly feel nerves like that again?"

The gig, in front of 80,000 people, led to a high-profile 2026 tour with pop-rock group McFly.

"Our dressing room was next to theirs at Wembley Stadium," Hull told presenter Steph Nieuwenhuys on BBC Introducing Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight.

"We just hit it off... We just toured the whole summer with them. Their crowds are crazy.

"It's scary being launched brand new into this industry without really knowing what we were doing.

"They've kind of taken us under their wing and been like: 'We'll look after you, you've got this.'"

Remember Monday's debut album, Can We Press Rewind?, is another "terrifying-slash-exciting" moment, according to Byrne.

Pre-released singles include the latest, Dream Cheat, a playful riff on the "relatable" experience of having a nightmare that a partner has been unfaithful.

Entertainment.title: Rob Brydon says he invented his own fake agent to negotiate fees
Entertainment.text:
Rob Brydon has revealed he pretended to be his own agent at the start of his career when he was working as a TV and radio presenter in Wales.

The actor, best known for playing Stacey's Uncle Bryn in the hit sitcom Gavin and Stacey, told BBC One's Graham Norton Show, external he used to step into the role of his fake agent to arrange bookings for events.

"I would get asked to go and do things, and I didn't really have an agent at that time so I invented a guy called Richard Knight," Brydon told the show.

The fictional agent would phone organisers and negotiate a fee for Brydon's appearance, he said.

The actor, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, shared an anecdote about being invited to a fundraiser and managing to get a fee for it.

"I'm terribly embarrassed," he told the show's host and fellow guests Cynthia Erivo, David Tennant and Laura Linney.

"They were all there for the good of their hearts," he said.

Brydon, known for his ability to mimic a range of celebrities, went on to impersonate the fictional Richard Knight asking for money in return for an appearance, with the agent describing Brydon as "an angel".

"I would go to these events and they would say 'oh I spoke to Mr Knight, he's quite a character', and I would say 'more than you realise'," Brydon told the show.

The 61-year-old actor stars in new sitcom Bill's Included in which he plays Bill Beam, a divorced man who rents his spare rooms to four students to stay financially afloat while "trying his very best to be their friend".

He told the Press Association he was drawn to his latest comedy role because he had missed acting in sitcoms since featuring in Gavin and Stacey.

The popular show ended in January 2010, although Christmas specials aired in 2019 and 2024.

While Brydon has since hosted shows including Destination X and Would I Lie To You?, the new show marks his return to the sitcom format.

"He calls himself a land-friend, not a landlord," Brydon said of his character Bill Beam.

Entertainment.title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
Entertainment.text:
Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.

The actress wrote on Instagram, external how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".

"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"

She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."

In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."

Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.

"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."

The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".

"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."

She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".

"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, external, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.

"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.

In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".

"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."

She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.

"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.

"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.
