EntertainmentTab.title: Babydoll singer Jamie Miller covers It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas
EntertainmentTab.text:
After spending four weeks at number one in the UK singles charts, Jamie Miller is releasing his take on the festive classic It's Beginning To Look A Lot Like Christmas.

In October, Miller became the first artist from Wales to top the UK singles chart since 2011 with his TikTok-viral song Babydoll.

The success transformed Miller's career, but he revealed that his "made it" moment was telling his taxi driver dad and cleaner mum they could retire.

While Babydoll's popularity continues, Miller teased the release of his next track on social media, telling fans: "You guys asked for a Christmas song..."

His cover arrives as artists compete for this year's Christmas number one.

Among those in the running is singer Sam Fender, who covered the Rolling Stones' You Can't Always Get What You Want in this year's John Lewis Christmas advert.

Other festive releases include Olivia Rodrigo's original Christmas song Take me Home (4 Christmas).

Classic Christmas songs also tend to return to the charts in the lead-up to the holiday, like the 1984 Wham! hit Last Christmas which is currently sitting at number 22.

The song made history in 2023 when, 39 years after release, it reached the Christmas number one spot for the first time, only to do so again the following year.

Regardless of the outcome of the Christmas charts, it is clear the success of Babydoll has had an enormous impact on the singer's life.

He previously shared with the BBC that "nothing feels normal" after the success of the track.

The star said Babydoll came after "a really, really hard few years in my personal life" and with almost 10 years of trying to make it in the industry, he had decided to give it one "last chance".

Miller praised his mum, Anne, when he appeared on the podcast The Person Who Believed in Me for her unwavering support.

He said that, during his childhood, other boys were interested in football and rugby, and there was "bullying" that came with pursuing singing.

But he said his mum would encourage him to "just to ignore people and to keep going".

"She's just the best thing that's ever happened to me," Miller said.

He also credited Anne for helping him get out of the "dark headspace" he was in some years ago: "There was a point where I didn't want to be here anymore. Being in that mind-frame was really scary."

He said she flew to the United States where he was living to spend time with him, and her love for him, expressed in "going on beach walks, going to grab me a coffee, pulling me out of bed", was what "got him out".

Miller also disclosed that money was something he had worried about throughout his life, adding the moment he knew he had "made it" was when he earned enough to help his parents retire.

The singer said his mum had "served everybody else for so long" and talked excitedly about calling her to say: "By the way mum, you never have to work again."

Miller said his mum was a cleaner who suffered from arthritis, and all he wanted to do was "take those products out of her hands and give her the life she deserves".

EntertainmentTab.title: Percy Jackson returns as teenage stars adapt to the limelight
EntertainmentTab.text:
Percy Jackson is no ordinary teenager - and neither is the actor tasked with bringing the character to life.

As the son of Greek god Poseidon, Percy has demigod status in the hit Disney series and while Walker Scobell doesn't have his powers, that hasn't made the actor's career any less special.

The TV series, based on the novels by Rick Riordan, sets figures from Greek mythology and their children in the modern day and returns on Friday for its third instalment - The Titan's Curse.

Scobell was 14 when he made his debut as Percy in 2023. Now 17, the US actor says growing up in the spotlight has been an adventure in itself.

"There's an upside for each downside," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

"It's a lot easier to get a table at restaurants now and you get to make people's days who are huge Percy Jackson fans just by talking to them for a few minutes. And I think that's a special part of it."

But it's not the only part.

Earlier this year, Scobell posted on Instagram that he would not be attending his school prom because of death threats sent to girls who live near him.

His co-star Aryan Simhadri, who plays Percy's best friend Grover Underwood, has also mentioned uncomfortable meetings with fans.

In an interview with Entertainment Weekly, external, he spoke about how "about 40 drunk college girls" recognised him and one tried to put her hand in his back pocket.

Since then, he says "fame hasn't been too bad, I've been able to have a normal life because of my parents".

"They really make sure when I'm not filming, I'm grounded and I'm planning for my future instead of being enamoured with the aspects of fame."

The new series is the first time The Titan's Curse has been adapted on screen.

An earlier film adaptation starring Logan Lerman only reached The Sea of Monsters, the second novel in the five-part series.

So the cast say they're in uncharted territory for the project - which sees Percy and Grover trying to rescue Annabeth from Kronos's forces.

"We can make the season in our own weird way because there's nothing you can compare it to, only the book," says Scobell.

"So it's the first time we're seeing any of this stuff."

Fans have been speculating online what to expect, especially after a shock diversion from the novel at the end of the last series.

"I think both book readers and non-book readers are going to be excited and appreciate the tone shift," Simhadri says.

"It changes how serious the world is, it's really the start of a new show, not to be dramatic."

It's caused a split in opinion from the fanbase, with one fan noting "they are going to stick to the books", but another saying "this is a twist they can get down with".

EntertainmentTab.title: How does Blackpool get ready to host Strictly Come Dancing?
EntertainmentTab.text:
Long before the sequins start to sparkle under the lights and the judges prepare to lift their paddles to deliver their scores, Blackpool Tower Ballroom is a hive of activity.

I have arrived here before Strictly Come Dancing returns to our screens from the famous ballroom.

While instantly recognisable, the venue is very different from what BBC One viewers will see on Saturday night.

Instead of dancers taking to the floor, a team of production crew is taking over with a different kind of choreography.

Standing beneath the lighting rig, I find myself looking up rather than down at the famous dance floor. Above me are hundreds of lights, hoisted into position days before anyone steps on to the set.

It is only when I sit in the balcony that the scale of the operation becomes clear. Camera tracks snake across the room, crews move between rehearsals, and every few minutes somebody is testing a new cue.

Blackpool week has become one of the most eagerly anticipated dates in the Strictly calendar.

Contestants spend weeks hoping they will survive long enough to perform beneath the ballroom's famous chandeliers, while fans look forward to the spectacular routines that the venue has become known for.

It's Olympic skeleton racing champion and Strictly contestant Tabby Stoecker's first time in Blackpool.

"Everyone has been describing the ballroom but I can't believe I get to dance in here," she says.

"I don't have words for this - it's so ornate and beautiful."

Fellow contestant Graeme Hall, also known as The Dog Father, says he has been "thinking of all the dancers who have been on this iconic floor, and now that'll be us on Saturday night".

The ballroom is a landmark in its own right, attracting visitors from around the world, but for one week each year it becomes the centre of one of the BBC's biggest shows.

By Saturday night, the cables will be hidden, the equipment will fade into the background and the focus will be firmly on the celebrities competing for a place in the next round.

But after seeing what is involved in bringing Strictly to Blackpool, it is very clear that the production off the dance floor is almost as impressive as what happens on it.

You can watch Strictly Come Dancing on BBC One from 18:35 GMT on Saturday

EntertainmentTab.title: Remember Monday 'still feel nerves' after Eurovision
EntertainmentTab.text:
Remember Monday used to say that representing the UK at the 2025 Eurovision Song Contest was the "scariest" moment of their career.

But an upcoming album and UK tour will send the adrenaline soaring again, according to members Holly-Anne Hull, Charlotte Steele and Lauren Byrne.

"We still feel nerves like it all the time," Hull told BBC Introducing.

The vocal trio have recorded a new session for the programme, which was the first to play their music on the radio in 2019.

Seven years on, their credits include festivals, singles and the Eurovision final, where they came 19th out of 28 countries.

"We're always feeling nerves like it," Hull said.

"About a month later, we were performing at Wembley Stadium and we were like, 'I can't take it'," Byrne recalled.

"How can you possibly feel nerves like that again?"

The gig, in front of 80,000 people, led to a high-profile 2026 tour with pop-rock group McFly.

"Our dressing room was next to theirs at Wembley Stadium," Hull told presenter Steph Nieuwenhuys on BBC Introducing Hampshire, Dorset and the Isle of Wight.

"We just hit it off... We just toured the whole summer with them. Their crowds are crazy.

"It's scary being launched brand new into this industry without really knowing what we were doing.

"They've kind of taken us under their wing and been like: 'We'll look after you, you've got this.'"

Remember Monday's debut album, Can We Press Rewind?, is another "terrifying-slash-exciting" moment, according to Byrne.

Pre-released singles include the latest, Dream Cheat, a playful riff on the "relatable" experience of having a nightmare that a partner has been unfaithful.

EntertainmentTab.title: Rob Brydon says he invented his own fake agent to negotiate fees
EntertainmentTab.text:
Rob Brydon has revealed he pretended to be his own agent at the start of his career when he was working as a TV and radio presenter in Wales.

The actor, best known for playing Stacey's Uncle Bryn in the hit sitcom Gavin and Stacey, told BBC One's Graham Norton Show, external he used to step into the role of his fake agent to arrange bookings for events.

"I would get asked to go and do things, and I didn't really have an agent at that time so I invented a guy called Richard Knight," Brydon told the show.

The fictional agent would phone organisers and negotiate a fee for Brydon's appearance, he said.

The actor, who grew up in Baglan, Port Talbot, shared an anecdote about being invited to a fundraiser and managing to get a fee for it.

"I'm terribly embarrassed," he told the show's host and fellow guests Cynthia Erivo, David Tennant and Laura Linney.

"They were all there for the good of their hearts," he said.

Brydon, known for his ability to mimic a range of celebrities, went on to impersonate the fictional Richard Knight asking for money in return for an appearance, with the agent describing Brydon as "an angel".

"I would go to these events and they would say 'oh I spoke to Mr Knight, he's quite a character', and I would say 'more than you realise'," Brydon told the show.

The 61-year-old actor stars in new sitcom Bill's Included in which he plays Bill Beam, a divorced man who rents his spare rooms to four students to stay financially afloat while "trying his very best to be their friend".

He told the Press Association he was drawn to his latest comedy role because he had missed acting in sitcoms since featuring in Gavin and Stacey.

The popular show ended in January 2010, although Christmas specials aired in 2019 and 2024.

While Brydon has since hosted shows including Destination X and Would I Lie To You?, the new show marks his return to the sitcom format.

"He calls himself a land-friend, not a landlord," Brydon said of his character Bill Beam.

EntertainmentTab.title: Florence Pugh hits out at weight loss and cosmetic surgery speculation
EntertainmentTab.text:
Florence Pugh has said she was "disturbed" to see "thousands of people" discussing her recent appearance at the Governors Awards, and denied speculation about weight-loss drugs and facial surgery.

The actress wrote on Instagram, external how "stressful" it was waking up to people "talking about you and your body in ways that you can't even comprehend".

"I have never been on Ozempic. I have never done any face surgery," she wrote. "And don't ever say that I didn't make my own nose, I've always had that beautiful ski slope. Even as a baby!"

She added: "For the first time in my entire career, I have had the opportunity to be rested, to sleep, to wake up and work out and to eat regularly and healthily."

In her eight-page statement, the Oppenheimer, Dune and East of Eden star told followers: "I'm looking after myself, and that's literally it."

Pugh highlighted that losing weight had not been her goal, and she had lost "two pounds".

"The thing that's most important to me and my trainer is muscle," she said. "I think it's the most important thing a woman can do. Build muscle and be strong. I can now do six pull-ups and lift 110kg.

"Which I'm sure to many of you isn't a lot... but to me?! It's everything."

The actress said that from the moment she entered the acting industry she was "subjected to fat shaming".

"I have loved every time I get to tell someone they are being inappropriate about my weight, and I'm not changing that now just because you've all said so."

She also said she was "disturbed" that "women who now think that I'm someone I'm not, for having my body dissected and pointed at again".

"I have spent my whole career defending and protecting bodies that just grow the way they grow."

Professor Heather Widdows from Everyday Lookism, external, which campaigns to end body shaming, told BBC News: "Pugh is right that we are in a place where 'beauty standards are changing, getting harder and harder to keep up with'.

"A global beauty ideal makes impossible demands and normalises what were once extreme," added Widdows, who is Professor of Philosophy at the University of Warwick.

"We know that body-shaming individuals is harmful. Given this, we should not say negative things about other people's bodies... in a world where our bodies are increasingly ourselves, when you shame bodies you shame people."

Pugh, who was Oscar-nominated for Little Women in 2020 and played Black Widow assassin Yelena Belova in this year's Spider-Man: Brand New Day, has previously spoken out against judgement about women's looks.

In 2024, she told the Times, external she aimed to "challenge how women were perceived".

"Look, not everybody has legs that go on for days. I remember watching this industry and feeling that I wasn't represented," she said. "I've loved challenging ideas I don't like."

She also spoke about why she thinks she receives criticism about her appearance.

"I've always been aware that seeing a confident woman be happy in her skin is triggering to a lot of people and for a long time just accepted that I will receive commentary like that," she said.

"But now this...? I'm asking us all to just be mindful. We are real people, living real lives."

Pugh did not have comments turned on for her post, but it was liked by celebrities including Ashley James, who is known for speaking out about body positivity, plus Carol Vorderman, Zoe Ball, writer and actress Katy Brand and doctor and broadcaster Amir Khan.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘It’s peak Aussie – and it’s fantastic!’ How Australian TV conquered the world
EntertainmentTab.text:
About four years ago, parents around the world began observing a strange phenomena in their children: Australian accents. Bluey – the charming cartoon about a dog and her family that is currently one of the most watched shows in the world – had children saying words such as “dunny” and “brekky” without thinking twice.

“When I was a kid, I would do an American accent when I played with my toys,” says Daley Pearson, co-founder of Ludo Studio, which makes Bluey. “So this is like the colony taking back over!”

In the last five years, Australia has staged a global cultural invasion via television. Count just the recent successes: Colin from Accounts, My Brilliant Career, Fisk, The Narrow Road to the Deep North, Dalliance, The Newsreader, Reckless, Goolagong, Territory, The Twelve, Apple Cider Vinegar, High Country, Love on the Spectrum, Last Seen, Mix Tape, Do Not Watch This Show, The Airport Chaplain, The Artful Dodger, Dog Park, Gnomes, Austin, Deadloch – and of course, a certain blue heeler. In the coming months, Brits will also get the outback thriller Treasure & Dirt (BBC), the true-crime documentary 2.6 Seconds (Netflix), the Anna Torv-led mystery Dustfall (BBC), as well as more Austin and Scrublands (BBC).

“It’s peak Aussie – and it’s fantastic,” as Amanda Duthie, Netflix’s head of content for Australia and New Zealand (My Brilliant Career, Apple Cider Vinegar), puts it.

“There’s people looking over the fence at us, saying: ‘What’s in the water in Australia at the moment?’” says Jennifer Collins, director of screen at the ABC, Australia’s national broadcaster (Love on the Spectrum, Bluey, Fisk, Austin, Dog Park). “Back in the day, kids’ shows and one or two dramas would do really well for us – but now all of our shows are cutting through.”

“I’ve been in the industry quite a while – some may say too long – but I remember the olden days when it was hard to get a pitch meeting with the UK commissioners and there weren’t that many Australian shows picked up there,” says Ian Collie, founder of production company Easy Tiger (Colin from Accounts, The Twelve, Scrublands, Territory). “But definitely in the last three or five years, there has been an upward trend, which is great.”

The question is: why? Is Australian TV getting better? Is there more of it? Or are international broadcasters and streaming services finally catching up to a good thing?

After speaking to more than a dozen producers, stars, directors and executives across Australia’s TV industry, the consensus is that something started changing 10 years ago, but really sped up around 2020. Covid lockdowns meant that the many talented Australians who had left for entertainment jobs in Hollywood and London fled home as work dried up. Everyone who used to moan about having to live in Los Angeles realised they didn’t need to any more.

“Actors now audition from a distance. Writing teams are scattered across the globe. Shows that are shot in England can be edited in Australia, or vice versa,” says Andy Ryan, head of drama at Australian streamer Stan (Scrublands, The Killings at Parrish Station, The F Ward). “That’s an unintended benefit of Covid for Australians – you don’t have to travel halfway around the world to have a meeting any more.”

Suddenly, Australia had a brain gain: all the expertise built overseas began being shared on masse. Meanwhile, the international streamers – Disney+, Netflix, Prime Video – had set up shop and were funding local productions; Australia’s domestic streamers and broadcasters geared up to compete. Then the Hollywood strikes of 2023 happened, which coincided with the start of a huge, ongoing decline in TV production in the US and the UK. The streaming giants and big broadcasters started hunting furiously for readymade hits abroad that they didn’t need to fund.

“There’s been a massive contraction globally in the number of shows being made, so all buyers are looking for shows that they think stand out,” says Carly Heaton at Fremantle Australia (Heartbreak High, Wellmania). “Everywhere, we’re seeing different content than what we might have normally seen – the Brits are seeing more Aussie content, and vice versa.”

Shrinking budgets have also made Australia a lot more attractive to foreign streamers and broadcasters looking for co-productions, rather than funding a show themselves: Colin from Accounts, for instance, was produced by Easy Tiger and CBS – but that means it was shown on CBS in the US (as well as the BBC in the UK).

“Australia is very cost-competitive internationally,” says Ryan at Stan, which regularly partners with UK broadcasters. “We make TV for a great price.”

Australia has also benefited from one international success: Squid Game. When the South Korean show became a massive global hit, all the old wisdom around commissioning went out of the window.

“People thought that Brits wanted to see Brits, Aussies wanted to see Aussie,” says Heaton at Fremantle Australia .“But Squid Game was a massive hit globally, and with subtitles – who would have thought that would happen? No buyers would have braved that before.”

“Everyone is watching so much more international TV,” says Duthie at Netflix (the brave buyer of Squid Game). “We are open to subtitles now! Nobody can quite believe it – ‘Honey, come and watch this show, it’s called Squid Game!’ The audience has muscled up, along with the sector.”

As Australian TV spreads, there seems to be a growing realisation that we don’t just make soaps. We have our own period dramas (My Brilliant Career) and office comedies (Fisk) and war stories (The Narrow Road to the Deep North) and romcoms (Colin from Accounts), plus a wealth of entirely unique First Nations stories. Australia is exotic enough to be interesting, but not so foreign that it’s challenging. “We feel quite distinctive, a bit fresh – just like Scandi noir did 10 or so years ago,” says Collie. We’re having our time in the sun.”

“There is an inherent curiosity about who we are as a nation, as a culture. We are not here making a watered-down version of a British or American show,” adds Nakul Legha, head of scripted at Australia’s multicultural public broadcaster SBS (The Airport Chaplain).

Frankly, though, some of Australia’s recent international successes simply can’t be explained. “None of us knew that Fisk would take off in the way it did,” laughs Collins at ABC, which sold the show to Netflix internationally.

Liz Doran was the showrunner on Netflix’s My Brilliant Career, which reached the Top 10 in 72 countries this year. The drama features a storyline where one character is implied to be part of the Stolen Generations – Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children forcibly removed from their families by the state – a historical point that is well known in Australia but not always abroad. “But we were never asked to add more dialogue to explain that, because we’re just treating the viewers like adults – if they’re curious, they’ll chase it,” Doran says. “Which is exactly what we have always done for shows from America.”

Australia is done explaining itself to the world: you figure out what a smoko or a bogan is if you care, hooroo. But the world seems to like that. When I recently interviewed Patrick Brammall and Harriet Dyer, the married creators and stars of Colin from Accounts, they recalled being asked by US executives to tweak an “arvo” in a script to “afternoon”. “And we were like … no,” Dyer told me. “It stayed in.”

“When Bluey took off, it felt like nobody cares any more – in a really great way,” says Pearson at Ludo. “People don’t need you to change things, they get it. That’s the stuff we loved about The Simpsons or John Hughes or the Beatles – they never pandered to you. People not only are happy to watch Australian stuff, they maybe even prefer it the more personal you go, the more foreign it feels.”

“What we’ve seen is when we’re hyperspecific in Australian content, that travels particularly well in the UK. Humour is an obvious shared sensibility,” says Alexandra Gilbert, head of content at Prime Video Australia and New Zealand (Deadloch, The Narrow Road). “Take something like Deadloch – a British audience might need a dictionary to translate half the words, but it travels incredibly well.”

“I’m quite sure most people don’t understand half the things the Heartbreak High kids are saying,” adds Heaton at Fremantle, which made the show for Netflix. “But you get the tone and, because of the specificity, it’s funny. And as long as you get the intent, you get the humour.”

“Specificity is hugely appealing,” adds Dena Curtis, head of Indigenous commissions and production at NITV, Australia’s Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander channel, which made Reckless. Although the show was based on a Scottish series (Guilt), Reckless is told from an Aboriginal perspective – “[which] is appealing overseas because that isn’t something that has been easily available,” Curtis adds. “It just takes one show to break through and then people say, OK – what else have you got?’ And I think it’s becoming anticipated that something coming out of Australia will be good.”

“I’m really mindful of the narrative that says: ‘Well, Australia is only starting to get good at making TV now!’ No!” says Legha. “We’ve had stories like The Flying Doctors, Wentworth, Rake, Kath & Kim, McLeod’s Daughters. We have an amazing history of great storytelling, I don’t think that’s changed. It is just that international buyers are seeing there is a real point of difference in the stories we’re telling here.”

“Everyone’s like, what’s the difference? It’s money,” says Doran. “I think one of the reasons some of our dramas haven’t travelled well in the past is because we are working on lower budgets than other countries. Australian crews and creatives are incredibly fast-paced and have initiative and we’ll work our arses off – but you can only make a low budget go so far. The international streamers mean we can make a show that has a polish and style on par with international shows.”

“Higher budgets don’t mean greater success; if only it was that easy!” counters Jo Porter, of production company Curio Pictures (High Country, The Artful Dodger, The Narrow Road). “But I think we’ve had to compromise in the past because we haven’t been able to finance at the level a particular story needed. Now we are able to prove our shows will sell globally, distributors have more confidence taking risks.”

A familiar face tends to inspire the UK to buy in particular: think Anna Friel in The F Ward, Ciarán Hinds and Jacob Elordi in The Narrow Road, David Thewlis in The Artful Dodger or Juliet Stevenson in Dustfall. Feral, a new Netflix drama, is filming in Queensland with Downton Abbey’s Michelle Dockery and Baby Reindeer’s Jessica Gunning; next year Sheridan Smith will lead Two Birds, a Stan and ITV co-production made in Western Australia.

“Marquee cast members do help sell the show internationally,” says Ryan. “And we’re not asking for them to come out to Australia for six months, more like four weeks. So it’s much more achievable from a logistics point of view. Also, 15 years ago, if you brought Anna Friel into an Australian medical show, you’d probably make a story point about why an English-accented doctor was in your hospital. Now we don’t explain it at all.”

So it is a bit of everything: a bit more money, a bit of pain overseas, a bit more openness internationally, and a lot of talent finally getting their dues. The phrase most often repeated was: “A rising tide lifts all boats.” Duthie at Netflix calls the current situation “a self-saucing pudding of confidence and opportunity: the more you do, the more you learn, the more you can deliver”.

“The Aussies are coming, watch out!” Collie laughs. “More than 200 years ago, the Brits sent all their riffraff to Australia. Now we’re coming to get them!”

EntertainmentTab.title: Melania: the series review – so bad it robbed me of my capacity to discern time and space
EntertainmentTab.text:
Previously on Melania: earlier this year – either because it found her a compelling subject, or because it wanted to flatter the president before a potentially destructive upcoming antitrust trial – Amazon spent $75m (£57m) to make and market a theatrically released documentary about Melania Trump.

I’m telling you this for two reasons. First, because you didn’t watch the Melania film. Nobody did, except for journalists who sat in otherwise empty cinemas and (if reports are to believed) people who responded to Craigslist ads offering them $50 to see it. The second reason is because Melania is a series now.

And, listen, I tried. I really tried to go into the series with an open mind. The first rule of criticism is that you should review what something is, and not what you want it to be. I was unable to do this, because I wanted it to be watchable, or to have any form of identifiable substance. In both cases, Melania came up wildly short.

Even calling it a series requires a wild stretching of the imagination. What we actually have here are two episodes, neither of which make it to the 40-minute mark, consisting of nothing but junky little offcuts that fail to tell us anything about anything. A lot of these episodes consist of Melania Trump flatly intoning the sort of empty platitudes found on AI-written CVs. For example, she understands that “meaningful action is driven by change”, which I’m sure will be a great relief to us all.

What a legitimately bizarre thing this is. Even its presentation is weird. Both episodes are full of the sort of faux-lifestyle shaky 8mm footage you’d expect to find on something like With Love, Meghan. It’s a trope you see when someone wants to inject a sense of homemade glamour into proceedings, except here a lot of this cutesy footage is actually of Arlington National Cemetery, home to thousands of dead American soldiers.

Then – and I promise that this isn’t an exaggeration – there is a sequence in the first episode where Melania deliberates about the exact placement of a brooch. This sequence goes on for so much longer than you would expect it to. While it was on, and she was agonising over the exact millimetre position of the brooch, I put the episode on 1.5x speed, and it still took for ever to finish. I ended up falling into a catatonic fugue state, watching it. I might still be watching it now. The show has robbed me of my capacity to discern the boundaries of time and space.

In truth, there is a single grain of substance here. The second episode sees Melania travel to North Carolina and California to meet victims of Hurricane Helene and the wildfires. When the camera pans around to hear the stories of the people who lost their homes, the series momentarily becomes human.

But that doesn’t last long, because it turns out that this was simply used as a way to leapfrog into a discussion about Melania’s work with foster children. Inevitably, her contribution to this involves saying the name of her website out loud in full, twice, then wanging on about the blockchain. Everything unstoppably, inevitably, goes back to her. At one point, the first assistant director shows Melania how his brother’s house was affected by the California fires. “This is all he packed,” he tells her sadly as he swipes through photos on his phone. “His guitars and his Maga hats.”

Calling Melania thin gruel would be an insult to the gruel industry. There are times when even the interviewer palpably gives up. He asks Melania how she unwinds, leading with a base-pleasing question about whether or not she prays. She shrugs it off with some woolly talk about how God is inside us. Does she go for long walks? “I don’t.” Instead, she reveals, she just goes to the spa a lot. “The first priority is to take care of yourself, so you can take care of other people,” she tells us, exactly as someone who tends not to care about other people very much would say. The exchange is Melania in microcosm.

But you’re not going to watch this either. Why would you? Melania is a dead-eyed advert that barely manages to masquerade as entertainment. It will leave you bored and depressed in equal measure. But, hey, so long as it helps with the antitrust trial.

EntertainmentTab.title: Roll up, roll up! Marc Chagall’s Circus is the most mesmerising big top you’ve ever seen – review
EntertainmentTab.text:
At the opening of The Circus, a self-portrait of Marc Chagall is placed next to a lithograph of a clown. The portrait is small and sketched simply in a blue crayon, as if Chagall had quickly dashed it out to pacify an inquisitive fan. In contrast, the clown is rich in colour and texture, with a heavily detailed backdrop of musicians, spectators and performers. But there is something uncanny about this pairing, created more than 40 years apart. They both wear small, brimmed hats with hair springing out from underneath, and their facial expressions are somewhat inscrutable.

It is the perfect introduction to an exhibition that explores Chagall’s lifelong fascination with the circus, both as a subject and as a symbolic motif. In placing Chagall and the clown side by side, we understand this immediately – the clown is both a clown and a metaphor for the artist. In his 1967 art book Cirque, Chagall writes: “This clown – he is he and I.”

Featuring more than 50 works, The Circus is a dazzling exploration of one of the 20th century’s most distinctive artists, delving into the way this magical arena and its cast of intriguing characters captured Chagall’s imagination, dancing across his canvases for more than 60 years. For Chagall, the circus is a mesmerising space beyond reality where it is possible to find childhood memories, artistic inspiration, spiritual enlightenment and both radiant light and deepest darkness.

The show includes his theatrical collaborations, paintings he produced in a box at the Cirque d’Hiver, pieces he made after his return to Paris after the second world war, and autobiographical works relating to Vitebsk, Russia, where he grew up. But shimmering at the heart of this exhibition is Cirque, an art book, large suite of lithographs and essay (newly translated into English for The Circus).

An entire, windowless space in a deep red is the setting for Cirque, which is presented here in its entirety. With the colourful lithographs popping off the walls, it feels as though I have disappeared into a big top. This is enhanced further by the decision to record Chagall’s Cirque essay, which is read by a French actor to give the language the artist’s accent. I pop on the headphones and for 24 minutes I am no longer in misty Wakefield but in the rafters of a tent watching hoops spin – or centre stage beside a ferocious lion.

The language in Cirque is as important as the visuals; as with Chagall’s art, where bodies float and animals shapeshift, so the text moves from a memory of street performers in Vitebsk, to the tail of a circus horse, to the story of Noah, to the greed of humanity. While I listen, I observe the vivid, swirling colours of a red leotard, a clown’s painted face and a bouquet of flowers. In many of the lithographs reality melts away – a moon bursts through the big top, a fish plays a drum, a Janus-faced figure plays music and weeps at the same time. For all their sparkling joy, each work features a looming audience, their round faces in rows, indistinguishable but heavily present, judging and reminding us of the outside world. Chagall’s words play through the headphones: “Alas, in life I have seen a ridiculous circus: someone thundered to terrify the world, and a thunder of applause answered him.” The circus is not all fun and games, on either side of the canvas.

The clever thing about placing Cirque at the start of the show is that it is then possible to follow these motifs through the rest of Chagall’s work, both before and after Cirque’s creation. The Four Heads – one of 19 paintings Chagall created from a box at the Cirque d’Hiver – was made in 1927 and, featuring a clown atop a many-headed creature, captures an early interest in the momentary spectacle of circus. Much later pieces from 1980 of his home in Vitebsk also include acrobats, lovers dancing and instrumentalists, indicating that these performing artists had inhabited his mind since childhood.

It is clear that for Chagall, performance and circus are inseparable. His work for Mozart’s The Magic Flute at the Metropolitan Opera in New York in 1967 involved set and costume design. The archival design pieces presented here again find flying figures, animals and instrumentalists – and that oppressive audience, sitting just beyond the performance, passing judgment on the art.

The challenge for any curator is to create a space that does justice to the spirit of the art on display. This is particularly hard when the subject is a supernatural display of magic, movement and artistry. But The Circus more than rises to the challenge, with thoughtful interventions that elevate the entire experience. From the ceiling fall two large, patchwork curtains by German artist Ulla von Brandenburg, which are pinned back with rope as if we are entering a circus tent and everyday life can surrender to the wonder of performance. In the centre of the gallery, a small inner room plays archive footage from the Cirque d’Hiver, encapsulating the stunning skills of the performers in real life.

Early on in his Cirque writing, Chagall asks: “These clowns, these bareback riders, these acrobats have taken up residence in my visions. Why?” We will never know the full answer, but certainly they imbued his art with the sensation that the world may be more than it first appears, and that can be a glorious thing.

GeneralTab.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
GeneralTab.text:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

GeneralTab.title: Dwain Hall found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby
GeneralTab.text:
A man has been found guilty of the kidnap and murder of a woman who he groomed on a fetish website.

Dwain Hall, 54, convinced 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Southsea, Hampshire, to travel to the United States where he stabbed her to death.

On Friday he was found guilty following a trial at a court in Ocala, Florida, of kidnap and first-degree murder. He was then sentenced to life in prison.

Exelby's body was found buried in Marion County, Florida, on 17 October 2025 after she was reported missing from her home five days earlier.

The trial of Hall, whose online username was Alpha Sadist, was told he had been the "executioner" of Sonia Exelby and had demanded she pay $4,000 (£3,000) for him to kill her.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

Hall was impassive as the unanimous verdict of the Florida jury was read out.

The court in Florida heard that the 32-year-old, who had struggled with mental illness, had wanted to die.

Assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said on the first day of the trial on Tuesday that Sonia Exelby met the defendant on a now-defunct website and "he manipulated her for years".

"He targeted her because of her mental illness and he exploited her for his own sadistic pleasure," she said.

"And when he finally got her alone, thousands of miles away from home, completely incapable of making any rational decisions, he stabbed her to death and buried her body."

Berndt said Exelby had been "trying to find someone who would kill her," adding: "Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible."

GeneralTab.title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing migrant dinghy
GeneralTab.text:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.

Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.

His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.

Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.

He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.

The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.

He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.

It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".

Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".

He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".

After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.

GeneralTab.title: Andy Burnham: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal
GeneralTab.text:
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".

Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.

Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.

The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.

The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.

The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.

There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."

The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.

Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".

He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.

Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.

"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."

Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.

The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.

Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".

Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".

Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".

She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".

Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."

In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

GeneralTab.title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
GeneralTab.text:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.

In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.

And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.

The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".

Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".

Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?

This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.

This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.

However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.

No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.

Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.

In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.

But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.

The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.

Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.

The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.

The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.

Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".

Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.

A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.

This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.

The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.

Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.

The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.

There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.

The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.

Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.

The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.

The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

articles.title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
articles.text:
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.

Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.

The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".

The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.

Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.

He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.

Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.

A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.

"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.

Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.

UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".

In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".

European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.

The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.

At least eight people were killed on Friday as Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.

This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.

Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.

Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.

The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

articles.title: Dwain Hall found guilty of kidnapping and murdering Sonia Exelby
articles.text:
A man has been found guilty of the kidnap and murder of a woman who he groomed on a fetish website.

Dwain Hall, 54, convinced 32-year-old Sonia Exelby from Southsea, Hampshire, to travel to the United States where he stabbed her to death.

On Friday he was found guilty following a trial at a court in Ocala, Florida, of kidnap and first-degree murder. He was then sentenced to life in prison.

Exelby's body was found buried in Marion County, Florida, on 17 October 2025 after she was reported missing from her home five days earlier.

The trial of Hall, whose online username was Alpha Sadist, was told he had been the "executioner" of Sonia Exelby and had demanded she pay $4,000 (£3,000) for him to kill her.

Warning: This article contains distressing details

Hall was impassive as the unanimous verdict of the Florida jury was read out.

The court in Florida heard that the 32-year-old, who had struggled with mental illness, had wanted to die.

Assistant state attorney Amy Berndt said on the first day of the trial on Tuesday that Sonia Exelby met the defendant on a now-defunct website and "he manipulated her for years".

"He targeted her because of her mental illness and he exploited her for his own sadistic pleasure," she said.

"And when he finally got her alone, thousands of miles away from home, completely incapable of making any rational decisions, he stabbed her to death and buried her body."

Berndt said Exelby had been "trying to find someone who would kill her," adding: "Unfortunately there was no shortage of depraved men willing to kill Sonia in the most torturous and vile ways possible."

articles.title: Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas jailed for slashing migrant dinghy
articles.text:
Anti-migrant activist Daniel Thomas has been jailed for 15 months for slashing a dinghy with a knife in the English Channel.

The 37-year-old, known to his supporters as Danny Tommo, live-streamed himself cutting the boat while a French rescue worker was on board in September.

Sentencing him after he admitted criminal damage, a judge called Thomas a "publicity seeker" whose actions were a "flagrant interference" with the work of rescue crews.

His barrister argued it was an act of "performative activism" rather than a "political crime" and said nobody had been put in danger.

Thomas founded the anti-migrant group Patriot Platform, which was behind protests in Portsmouth and Dover involving masked men in September.

He appeared at Portsmouth Crown Court by video link from HMP Winchester, and sat with his head in his hands for much of the hearing.

The court heard he had watched migrants being taken off the dinghy by the RNLI, Border Force and the French Coastguard on 22 September, before telling those on his boat to steer towards it.

He said "let's get rid of that boat" before slashing it about eight times, the court heard.

It had previously been reported that Thomas said "this is what needs to happen to everyone in these boats" in his live-stream of the incident, but the court heard on Friday that he said "this is what needs to happen to every one of these boats".

Earlier in the footage, Thomas told viewers "no violence, nothing like that" and urged them to "share this everywhere".

He gave a postcode in Gosport, which the judge said he believed was to "encourage protest".

After slashing the boat, he shouted at the rescue worker: "Get off the boat, you've got time to get off the boat," the court heard.

articles.title: Calls for consent defence change after Joanne Young rape case
articles.text:
The daughter of Joanne Young, who was drugged, raped and advertised for sex online by her husband, is among those calling for a change in the way cases are defended in court.

Philip Young drugged and abused his wife over a 13-year period, using websites and apps to invite men to their home in Swindon without her knowledge. On Thursday, four men were found guilty of sexual offences against her.

The trial has sparked calls for the government to ensure defendants cannot use "third-party consent" as a defence in rape trials.

Daughter Alex Young said: "It has been 23 years since this was last updated. Society has progressed, crime has progressed. So why hasn't the law progressed with it?"

Warning: This story discusses sexual violence and abuse

Philip Young advertised his wife for sex using websites such as Craigslist, Grindr and FabSwingers without her knowledge.

During the trial, the prosecution stated that the four men, who were all strangers to each other, failed to seek consent from Joanne Young before they engaged in sexual activity with her.

The defendants claimed they had been duped by Philip Young and believed she was consenting.

The Sexual Offences Act 2003 states that "a person consents if he agrees by choice, and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice".

There is no defined law which states third-party consent is a valid defence.

In a post on LinkedIn, Alex Young said: "We live in a world where there is debate over whether third-party consent is enough to have sex with someone... and that is enough to use it as an argument in a court of law.

"This is simply unacceptable."

Her calls echo those made by her mother, who spoke on the steps of Winchester Crown Court after the trial.

"No-one should be able to give it [consent] on your behalf," said Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.

"I urge the government to look at this as a priority so that women are properly protected in future."

Kate Parker, criminal barrister and founder of the Schools Consent Project, said legally, a third party or a partner cannot consent on a person's behalf.

"The law makes that very clear. A person consents if he or she agrees by choice and has the freedom and capacity to make that choice," she added.

"In a case like this where someone has been made unconscious, there is no possible way that that person is able to consent because of course they have no capacity."

She added that the defendants' claims that they thought Joanne Young had consented through her husband "doesn't make sense legally, and that's not a legal position that can be supported in court".

Parker said the defence used by the four men in the trial is not a correct application of the law but might be something defence lawyers would try and rely on as their client's genuine belief in their victim's consent, or in mitigation to try and get a lower sentence.

Like Joanne Young, Laura Bishop from Bristol has also waived her right to anonymity after her ex-husband received a 14-year prison sentence for drugging and raping her while inviting other men to abuse her.

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, Bishop said the crimes will affect her for the rest of her life.

"It's something that unfortunately you can never get over," she said.

"You have to try and remain positive and optimistic but the betrayal, particularly by men, is very difficult to move on from."

Bishop has a PhD in cyber crime and uses her expertise and experience to work with MPs and charities to improve governance around digital safety and regulations.

"The sites my husband used to advertise me are still active and are known by the police to not provide evidence and forensics when asked.

"So why are they still accessible?" she said.

Bishop understands why many choose to maintain their anonymity but wants to encourage those who can speak out to do so.

"There's a million reasons why its not be appropriate to waive your anonymity and it might just be because it's something you can't actively do," she said.

"But for those of us that are able to, we have to stand strong for victims."

Debbie Beadle, chief executive officer at Wiltshire-based domestic abuse charity Fear Free, also hopes that Joanne Young's decision to speak out will encourage others to do so.

"Six in seven rapes against women are done by someone they know and this adds a barrier to people coming forward," she said.

"The fact that Joanne has come forward will help others when this has happened to them."

Zoe Watts is the founder of a global campaign called End Eye Check that works to raise awareness of drug-facilitated sexual abuse.

Like Joanne Young and Bishop, Watts waived her right to anonymity after she was drugged and raped by her husband.

Watts hopes that Joanne Young's case "sets a precedent", but told Woman's Hour that the crime is more widespread than many realise.

"I have had women contact me from 25 different countries," she said.

"It's a daily process of women either contacting me because they've woken up to find their husband having sex with them while they're asleep and have done on numerous occasions.

"Or perhaps they're not sure if they've been drugged or maybe they are genuinely asleep and wake up and find him that way, or women that have found videos or recordings on their phone of things they haven't consented to," Watts added.

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, support and information is available at BBC Action Line.

Professor Miranda Horvath, director of the University of Suffolk's Institute for Social Justice and Crime, told the BBC that more needs to be done to tackle and "de-platform" perpetrators.

"The research being conducted and the evidence base we have is emerging [because] these kinds of offences are under-reported and under-detected," she said.

"We need to ensure proper implementation of the legislation we have through suspect-focused investigation, prosecutions and resourcing and training of the professionals working in these environments.

"[We also need to be] holding the platforms and tech firms to account that are continuing to proliferate this material and saying 'this is enough, we will not tolerate this in our society'."

Prosecutors said Thursday's trial was the first of its kind in England, but former minister for safeguarding and violence against women and girls, Jess Phillips, told Radio 4's Woman's Hour that current laws do not do enough to protect women.

"The law says that somebody can seek a defence to defend themselves against a rape claim if they reasonably believe that they had consent," said Phillips.

"These people went on to argue that they reasonably believed that Joanne's husband had sought her consent and got it.

"They were found guilty, but it's whether the law needs to explicitly say, 'you cannot reasonably believe someone's given consent unless they have given it'.

"If there was clarity in the law, Joanne wouldn't have been put through the court case," Phillips added.

She also believes that more needs to be done to hold the websites hosting adverts and similar content to account.

"Can every pornographic site in our country categorically say that not one of these snuff videos or sedated videos is on their site?

"Unless they can guarantee it with a signed piece of paper from the person that they know is in that video [they should not be published]," Phillips said.

Sarah Hammond, the chief crown prosecutor at the CPS who oversees many complex sexual offence cases involving drugs, said Joanne's "incredibly powerful" statement after the convictions "laid bare the devastating impact of the horrific abuse she had suffered over so many years".

"A lot of people may not know exactly what consent means in law, but the principle is simple. Consent must be a free choice made by someone who has the freedom and capacity to make it, and nobody else can give consent on their behalf," she said.

"In this case, the evidence proved that not only did Joanne not consent to the sexual activity, but that the perpetrators could not reasonably believe that she was consenting.

"This meant asking what steps the perpetrators had taken to establish consent for themselves, rather than relying on assumptions or what somebody else had told them.

"The convictions of Philip Young, Dean Hamilton, Norman Macksoni, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins and Mohammed Hassan send a clear message: consent is something you establish with the person themselves, and where someone is drugged or otherwise incapacitated, they cannot make that choice."

Wiltshire Police Supt Int Geoff Smith, the lead investigating officer in the case, said he hoped the guilty verdicts made women feel "safer".

"I hope that men take note about seeking consent and what's required from them, and I hope that women feel more able and confident to come forward and speak out," he said.

"I really hope it makes a difference."

articles.title: St Mellons fatal crash police officers sacked for lying over searches
articles.text:
Two officers who lied about carrying out missing person searches linked to a crash in which three people died have been sacked after being found guilty at a police misconduct hearing.

PC Richard Hardwick and PC Lauren Livingstone faced gross misconduct allegations over their actions before a car carrying five people was found crashed two days later in St Mellons, Cardiff, in 2023.

The hearing in Newport was told they were "dishonest" in official logs and to a senior officer by claiming searches of the homes of Eve Smith, who died, and Sophie Russon had been carried out.

Members of Smith's family described the verdict as "an important step towards accountability".

Following the proceedings, Smith's mother Emma Borg said the family had to repeatedly revisit the "most painful period" of their lives.

She said her family felt their honesty and credibility was being "questioned" at a time when they "trusted the police to do their jobs".

"Instead, the dishonesty established during these proceedings undermined the missing persons' investigation and the trust our families desperately needed to have in those responsible for helping us," she added.

Lauren Doyle, Smith's sister, said they "never wanted to spend years scrutinising police decisions" and called the outcome of the proceedings an "important step".

She added: "Our search for answers continues. We will never lose sight of why we started."

The police watchdog call the officers' actions "inexcusable with both failing in the fundamental basics of policing".

Panel chairman Ian Arundale said a final written warning was not an option because the level of harm and culpability was too high. He also said there was a lack of mitigating factors.

Hardwick and Livingstone had deliberately misled a missing persons investigation, he added, which may have compromised the investigation, and had undermined public trust in the police in a high-profile case.

Hardwick faced six allegations, including that he lied about searching the homes of crash victims Smith and Russon, and that he also lied to his supervising officer and the police watchdog.

Livingstone faced four allegations, including that she lied about searching the two houses, as well as making a dishonest entry on the log and lying to her supervising officer.

The police disciplinary hearing at Rodney Parade, which lasted four days, was told that both officers were part of the team assigned to look into reports that Eve Smith, Darcy Ross and Sophie Russon had gone missing after a night out on Friday 3 March 2023.

The three women were reported missing to Gwent Police on 4 March, but were not found until 30 hours after the initial contact by the families.

Five people were found in a car in a wooded area off the A48, 46 hours after the vehicle had crashed.

Three of the cars occupants, Eve Smith, Rafel Jeanne, and Darcy Ross had died, and two, Sophie Russon and Shane Loughlin, were seriously injured.

Hardwick and Livingstone went to Russon's home and then on to Smith's house, and as part of Gwent Police's missing person policy were supposed to search the address to look for clues for what might have happened to them.

Hardwick wrote in the official log afterwards "premise search conducted" and told the police sergeant overseeing the case that the search at Russon's house had been carried out. He also said searches had happened when he spoke to the police watchdog, the IOPC, who later investigated.

This was in contrast to what Russon's father, Nathan, told the hearing, that the officers were at the house for a very short period and did not ask to search the bedroom.

Livingstone said she could not remember whether searches had taken place, but wrote what she agreed was a "poorly written" report in the official log, which the panel head heard was "deliberately vague" but suggested a search had taken place.

The panel found Hardwick and Livingstone had failed to conduct a search at Smith and Russon's homes.

Hardwick was found to have provided a false entry into the police log and had provided a dishonest statement when interviewed by the IOPC.

He had been found, in part, to have given a dishonest account of the search to his supervisor and found in part to have provided a dishonest account in a signed statement to the IOPC.

Livingstone was found to also have provided a false entry into the police log and to have had given a dishonest account of the search to her supervisor.

Panel chairman Ian Arundale said their behaviour had caused harm because of the impact on the family and had undermined public trust in the police in a case which resulted in significant levels of concern from the public.

Derrick Campbell, from the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said the officers failed to "act honestly and with integrity", saying property searches were a "basic but essential part in the early stages of a missing person investigation".

"PC Hardwick deliberately lied during the course of the missing person investigation, claiming on police records and to his supervisor that searches had been completed.

"PC Livingstone had ample opportunity to tell the IOPC the required searches had not been conducted.

"Instead, she did not give an account and stated she could not remember the specifics of her visits to the homes of two of the young women who had been reported missing," Campbell said.

articles.title: Texas death-row inmate screams as execution takes more than one hour
articles.text:
A US death row inmate has screamed in apparent pain during his Texas execution which lasted more than an hour.

This is "not working the way it should be," Reinaldo Dennes, 70, said as he was being injected with the drug pentobarbital, according to witnesses.

A spokeswoman for the Texas Department of Criminal Justice said there had been unsuccessful attempts to find veins for the injections, but added that Dennes had reported pain in parts of his body where there were no attempted injections.

Dennes's case comes weeks after the botched execution of Christa Pike, who survived two lethal doses and is believed to be the only individual to have survived an execution attempt by lethal injection.

Dennes was sentenced to death over the 1996 murder of Janos Szucs, a diamond dealer who was found shot multiple times.

His execution came on the same day another inmate was put to death in Florida.

Executions with a lethal drug usually last from a few minutes to over an hour.

Michael Graczyk, an Associated Press reporter who has witnessed many such executions, described how they had waited for an unusually long time before being taken into the chamber. According to him, such delays are usually due to an inmate resisting the procedure or difficulty in finding veins.

When the witnesses were finally allowed in, Dennes almost immediately exclaimed, "The pain! Go! Go!", Graczyk said. He then uttered an expletive and asked "the father" to "take this pain".

He then shouted: "My right leg is killing me!", describing it as a cramp. After another expletive, he grunted and said, "I don't think this is normal."

Another witness, the reverend Jeff Hood, told USA Today that Dennes's execution was "by far the worst one" he had seen.

"He [Dennes] screamed out, 'my leg, my leg, my leg'," Hood said. "He screamed out twice, 'it's not working like it's supposed to.'"
